items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: The printed shape can match Latin A. In this course it is the Cyrillic vowel letter А.
distractorRationales: The capital shapes can look the same, but this card belongs to the Cyrillic alphabet. Latin A is a letter of a different alphabet.
Р has a vertical stem and an upper loop. А has two sloping sides and a crossbar.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: М is an early consonant letter. It is not Н.
distractorRationales: Н has two upright strokes joined by a horizontal crossbar. М has inner diagonal strokes.
Т has a top bar and a central stem. It does not have the inner diagonal strokes of М.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin P. What is it?
items.feedback: Shape overlap with Latin P is a recognition trap. This is Cyrillic Р, not English P.
distractorRationales: The capital shapes can look the same, but this is a Cyrillic letter card. The Latin name P does not name the Russian letter.
П has two uprights joined across the top. Р has an upper loop attached to its stem.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin H. What is it?
items.feedback: Do not read Н as English H. It is a Cyrillic letter.
distractorRationales: The similar capital shape does not give this Cyrillic letter the Latin name H. Identify it within the Russian alphabet.
И joins its uprights with a diagonal. Н uses a horizontal crossbar instead.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin C. What is it?
items.feedback: С is a Cyrillic letter. Do not treat the Latin look-alike as the identity.
distractorRationales: The similar capital shapes belong to different alphabets. The Latin name C does not identify this Cyrillic letter.
К has diagonal arms extending from a straight stem. С is an open curved shape.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin B. What is it?
items.feedback: В is not Latin B and it is not Cyrillic Б.
distractorRationales: The Latin capital B looks similar, but this is a Cyrillic letter card. A Latin letter name does not identify it.
Б has a top horizontal stroke and one lower bowl. В has two bowls.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin Y. What is it?
items.feedback: У is a Cyrillic vowel letter, not Latin Y.
distractorRationales: The Latin capital Y may look similar, but this card belongs to the Cyrillic alphabet. Use the Cyrillic identity.
И has two upright strokes joined diagonally. У has an upper fork and a descending tail.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin X. What is it?
items.feedback: Х is a Cyrillic letter, not Latin X.
distractorRationales: The matching shape does not make this the Latin letter X. This card belongs to the Cyrillic alphabet.
К has a vertical stem with two arms. Х consists of two crossing diagonal strokes.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Ё is its own letter. Е and Э are different letters.
distractorRationales: Е has the same main shape but no dots. The two dots distinguish the shown Ё.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Ю is an iotated vowel letter. У and Я are different letters.
distractorRationales: У has an upper fork and a descending tail. Ю has an upright joined to a rounded part.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Я is an iotated vowel letter. It is not Р or А.
distractorRationales: Р has its loop on the right of the stem. Я has a loop on the left and a diagonal leg.

references.title: Cyrillic print forms
references.summary: 33 printed uppercase/lowercase pairs.
references.detail: Use the letter board grouped by the Unit 1 sequence. Use your book for English explanations of the sounds. No example words are attached.

references.title: Confusable Latin look-alikes
references.summary: В Н Р С У Х can be misread by Latin-alphabet readers.
references.detail: Name the Cyrillic identity. Confirm sounds in your book.

references.title: Iotated vowel letters
references.summary: Е Ё Ю Я are a recognition group in Unit 1.
references.detail: Use your book for detailed phonetics.

references.title: Soft sign, hard sign, and Й
references.summary: Ь and Ъ are signs. Й is not a standalone vowel in this foundation.
references.detail: Do not invent a spoken vowel for the signs. Use the book for the exact rule.
searchTerms: soft sign, hard sign, and й

references.title: Transliteration is temporary
references.summary: Latin respelling may help the first hours. It is not how you should keep reading.
references.detail: Turn transliteration off in settings as soon as print recognition is stable.

references.title: Staged decoding limits
references.summary: Practise recognising letters and matching their print pairs.
references.detail: Practise reading words, phrases and signs in your book.

references.title: Stress notation
references.summary: Learn each word’s stress as part of reading Russian.
references.detail: Copy stress marks from your book into your binder.

references.title: Pronunciation guidance
references.summary: Play model audio when it is available for the current topic.
references.detail: User recordings play at original speed. No ASR or score.

references.title: How to use this companion
references.summary: The app coordinates the book, optional AnkiDroid, a binder, and optional tutor work.
references.detail: It does not reproduce Penguin, judge spontaneous speech, or certify proficiency.

references.title: App limitations
references.summary: Offline only. No internet, no account, no AI, no cloud.
references.detail: Use your book for pronunciation practice alongside Units 1–2. The app does not score handwriting or pronunciation. Use your book for handwriting study. Review Unit 1 letters in Unit 2; study Lesson 3 grammar in your book. Continue using the available lessons and your own book.

references.title: Find a lesson
references.summary: Open a unit to find its available lessons.
references.detail: Choose a unit with available lessons. If a unit is unavailable, open the matching lesson in your own book. Open the matching lesson in the copy you own. Use this reference to find the matching lesson.

references.detail: Unit 1 letter names: А is named а; Б is named бэ; В is named вэ; Г is named гэ; Д is named дэ; Е is named е; Ё is named ё; Ж is named жэ; З is named зэ; И is named и; Й is named и краткое; К is named ка; Л is named эль; М is named эм; Н is named эн; О is named о; П is named пэ; Р is named эр; С is named эс; Т is named тэ; У is named у; Ф is named эф; Х is named ха; Ц is named цэ; Ч is named че; Ш is named ша; Щ is named ща; Ъ is named твёрдый знак; Ы is named ы; Ь is named мягкий знак; Э is named э; Ю is named ю; Я is named я.

references.title: Cases and the accusative
references.summary: How case marks a noun's role, the accusative of direct objects, animacy and object pronouns.
references.detail:
Case shows a noun's role in the sentence, so a Russian sentence relies less on word order than an English one. Compare Собаки ненавидят котов. — Dogs hate cats. with Коты ненавидят собак. — Cats hate dogs.

The accusative marks the direct object. Feminine nouns change the ending -а to -у and the ending -я to -ю; feminine nouns ending in the soft sign -ь do not change.

Masculine nouns follow animacy. An inanimate noun keeps its nominative form: Я де́лал стул. — I made a chair. An animate noun takes the same form as its genitive: Я люблю этого кота. — I like this cat. The form matches the genitive, but the noun is still the direct object.

Object pronouns: Я — I, Меня — me. Мы — we, Нас — us. Ты — you, Тебя — you. Вы — you, Вас — you. Он — he, Его — him. Она — she, Её — her. Они — they, Их — them.

Adjectives and possessives change to fit the noun they describe, taking on its gender, number and case.

references.title: Aspect
references.summary: Aspect pairs, the aspect of быть, and what an imperfective past means.
references.detail: Aspect pairs are bounded: not every verb has a partner, and each pair is learned as a pair. быть is imperfective. An imperfective past need not mean the event was unfinished.

references.title: Stress pairs and final consonants
references.summary: Words that differ only by stress, and words whose final consonants sound alike.
references.detail: за́мок (castle) and замо́к (lock), му́ка (torment) and мука́ (flour) differ only in the stressed vowel. луг (meadow) and лук (onion), код (code) and кот (cat), плод (fruit) and плот (raft) end in the same sound when said on their own, because a final г sounds like к and a final д like т.

references.title: Noun gender groups
references.summary: Each noun belongs to one of three groups; learn the group with the word.
references.detail:
So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. Learn each word with its group; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. учи́тель — teacher. друг — friend is also masculine. Learn the group with each word; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. ма́ма — mom. дверь — door is feminine too. Learn the group with each word; do not guess the group of another word from its ending.

These words are neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea.

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

references.title: Personal pronouns
references.summary: The person words я, ты, он, она́, оно́, мы, вы and они́ with their meanings.
references.detail:
я — I. мы — we.

ты — you. вы — you (plural).

он — he. она́ — she. оно́ — it. они́ — they.

references.title: Present-tense forms
references.summary: How the present is formed, with the forms of чита́ть and де́лать.
references.detail:
To form the present tense, add the appropriate endings to the verb. Verbs in Russian conjugate in one of two ways.

чита́ть in the present: I чита́ю, you чита́ешь, he чита́ет.

чита́ть in the present: we чита́ем, you (plural) чита́ете, they чита́ют.

де́лать — make. With I: де́лаю.

references.title: The nominative subject
references.summary: The dictionary form as the subject of a supplied sentence.
references.detail:
In the supplied Муж говорит, the husband is the subject and the talking verb states its action. The noun names the subject, in the nominative case. Distinguish the noun’s subject or direct-object role from the meaning of the sentence. Do not guess nominative merely because a case is unfamiliar.

In Поезд старый, the train is the subject noun and old is its predicate description. This present property clause has no overt Russian copula. The noun’s case role is nominative subject, not accusative direct object. A dictionary-looking noun or familiar translation alone does not identify its role in every construction.

Студент новый supplies a second independent property clause: the student is the subject noun, and new describes that subject. Its case role is nominative subject. Keep Муж говорит — The husband is talking and Поезд старый — The train is old as correct sentence meanings. Other constructions have nominative predicate nouns; not every nominative noun is a subject.

references.title: Question words
references.summary: Question words and written questions.
references.detail:
Кто — Who. Что — What. Когда — When. Почему — Why.

Как — How. Где — Where (location). Куда — where to.

Откуда — where from. Сколько — How much, how many. Какой — What kind.

Что это? — What is this?. Кто это? — Who is this?.

Как дела? — How do you do?/How're things?. Где вы живёте? — Where do you live?.

references.title: The prepositional
references.summary: Quoted about- and place-examples and the dictionary form pairs.
references.detail:
О книге — About the book. О письме — About the letter.

О саде — About the garden. я в Москве — I'm in Moscow.

Он на крыше — He's on the roof. Он в театре — He is at the theatre.

Ваза стоит на столе. — The vase stands on the table. Картина висит на стене. — The painting hangs on the wall.

Use these words only in the phrases shown. в — in. на — on (place). о — about.

Each pair shows the first form, then the second form of the same word. кни́га / кни́ге. письмо́ / письме́.

references.title: Indeclinable nouns
references.summary: Nouns that keep one form, contrasted with nouns that can change.
references.detail:
An indeclinable noun keeps the same form for case or number. In these examples, ра́дио and такси́ are indeclinable. Recognize the behavior of the shown noun.

The nouns метро́, кино́, пальто́ and ко́фе are also indeclinable. Their forms stay unchanged for case or number. Learn the noun with this behavior; do not infer that every noun with a similar ending behaves the same way.

кафе́ and меню́ are two more indeclinable nouns. An unchanged word form does not mean that a sentence has no case relationships.

Contrast кни́га and окно́: these nouns are declinable, so they can change for case. Their nominative and genitive forms differ. Choose the behavior of the shown noun: unchanged for case or number, or able to change for case. No new form needs to be invented.

references.title: Possessives
references.summary: My, your, our and his, her, their with the nouns they describe.
references.detail:
Possessives such as Мой, Твой, Наш and Ваш act like adjectives: they change to match the noun they describe, not the owner. Твой is the informal or singular your; Ваш is the formal or plural your.

In the accusative, my has the forms Мой and Моего (masculine, inanimate and animate), мою (feminine), Моё (neuter), and Мои and Моих (plural, inanimate and animate). Our follows the same pattern: Наш, Нашего, нашу, Наше, Наши, Наших.

The third-person possessives его (his), её (her) and их (their) do not change with the noun they describe: Я хочу его кота — I want his cat. Я хочу его котов — I want his cats.

references.title: Direction and location
references.summary: в and на with the accusative for direction and the prepositional for location.
references.detail:
With the accusative, в means to or into, and на means onto or toward: Я шёл в дом — I walked into the house. Я шёл на улицу — I walked onto the street.

With the prepositional case, в means in or at, and на means upon or at: Я жил в Лондоне — I lived in London. Оно на столе — It's on the table.

The accusative shows direction; the prepositional shows location.

references.title: Adjectives
references.summary: Dictionary form, agreement, spelling and case forms of adjectives.
references.detail:
The dictionary form of an adjective is masculine singular nominative, ending in -ый, -ий or -ой.

An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case: новый карандаш — new pencil; новая машина — new car; новое платье — new dress; эти хорошие новые студенты — these good new students.

Soft adjectives keep the soft ending: синий стол. — the dark blue table; синяя книга — the dark blue book; синее письмо — the dark blue letter; синие книги — the dark blue books.

Spelling: after г, ж, к, х, ч, ш or щ, write и rather than ы. After ж, ц, ч, ш or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е, as in хорошее письмо — the good letter.

како́й means which, what or what kind of. э́тот means this; its plural э́ти means these, as in эти хорошие новые студенты.

In the prepositional, masculine and neuter adjectives end in -ом (-ем after a soft ending or ш, щ, ч, ж, ц), feminine adjectives in -ой (-ей), and plural adjectives in -ых (-их): Она́ в си́ней кварти́ре, не в бе́лой кварти́ре — She's in the blue apartment, not the white apartment.

In the accusative, feminine adjectives end in -ую (-юю after a soft ending): Анна встретила новую учительницу. — Anna met the new teacher. Masculine and plural adjectives follow the animacy of their noun.

references.title: Adverbs
references.summary: What adverbs describe, why they do not change, and the two taught adjective and adverb pairs.
references.detail:
Adverbs describe a verb much like adjectives describe nouns.

Наречия — неизменяемые слова: adverbs do not decline or conjugate, and they do not change for gender or number. This does not mean that comparative forms cannot exist.

Two adjective and adverb pairs are taught here: быстрый — быстро and творческий — творчески. Learn each pair as it is taught.

references.title: Noun plurals
references.summary: Nominative plural endings, the seven-letter spelling rule, and plurals to learn as words.
references.detail:
Masculine nouns add -ы: стол — table, столы — tables. Feminine nouns ending in -а replace it with -ы: машина — car, машины — cars. Feminine nouns ending in -я or -ь take -и. Neuter nouns ending in -о take -а: письмо — letter, письма — letters.

After к, г, х, ш, щ, ж or ч, use -и instead of -ы. книга (book) has the stem книг-, so it follows this rule.

Some plurals are learned as words: Сын and Сыновья (son, sons); Брат and Братья (brother, brothers); Друг and Друзья (friend, friends).

Plural adjectives end in -ые or -ие; see Adjectives.

references.title: There is, there are
references.summary: есть with the nominative to say that something exists somewhere.
references.detail:
Есть can say there is or there are. It is followed by the nominative case.

На э́той у́лице есть францу́зы — There are Frenchmen on this street. В Москве́ есть ста́рые зда́ния — There are old buildings in Moscow.

The noun naming what exists is nominative; the place phrase is separate.

references.title: Numbers and counting
references.summary: Cardinal numbers, the forms of one and two, and the noun case after a number.
references.detail:
Numbers: 1 оди́н, 2 два, 3 три, 4 четы́ре, 5 пять, 6 шесть, 7 семь, 8 во́семь, 9 де́вять, 10 де́сять, 11 оди́ннадцать, 20 два́дцать, 100 сто, 1,000 ты́сяча. Compound numbers: два́дцать оди́н — 21; сто оди́н — 101; две́сти пятна́дцать — 215.

One agrees with its noun: один мальчик — one boy; одна девушка — one girl. Two is два with masculine and neuter nouns and две with feminine nouns.

In the nominative and the inanimate accusative, the last digit decides the noun's case. A number ending in один takes the nominative singular: Есть оди́н кот — There is one cat. A number ending in 2, 3 or 4 takes the genitive singular: Два рубля́ — Two roubles; Два́дцать две копе́йки — 22 kopecks. A number ending in 5 to 9 or 0, and every teen, takes the genitive plural: Пять рубле́й — Five roubles; Два́дцать пять копе́ек — 25 kopecks; шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles.

Above 99, the last two digits decide: двести три собаки — two hundred and three dogs; двести тринадцать собак — two hundred and thirteen dogs. In other sentence cases the number itself also changes.

references.title: Genitive nouns
references.summary: Genitive singular and plural noun endings used after numbers.
references.detail:
Genitive singular: masculine nouns ending in a consonant add -а, and -й or -ь becomes -я. Neuter -о becomes -а and -е becomes -я. Feminine -а becomes -ы, -я and -ь become -и, and after the seven consonants -а becomes -и.

Genitive plural, with the forms used after a number: Стол, пять столов — Table, five tables. Музе́й, шесть музе́ев — Museum, six museums. Вещь, десять веще́й — Thing, ten things. Неде́ля, семь неде́ль — Week, seven weeks. Кни́га, во́семь книг — Book, eight books.

The genitive plural has many exceptions; learn each new form as it is taught.

references.title: Having and not having
references.summary: у with the genitive and есть or нет to say what someone has or lacks.
references.detail:
To say someone has something, put the owner in the genitive after у and follow it with есть and the thing owned in the nominative: У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend.

To say that something is absent, use нет followed by the genitive: Нет рестора́нов — There are no restaurants. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

references.title: The genitive: pronouns, prepositions and adjectives
references.summary: Genitive pronouns, prepositions that take the genitive, genitive adjectives and animate plural objects.
references.detail:
Genitive pronouns: Я → Меня́, Мы → Нас, Ты → Тебя́, Вы → Вас, Он/она/оно → Его́/её, Они → Их. The genitive for of him and of it is the same, его́. After a preposition, его, её and их gain н, as in Для него́ — For him/it. Без неё — Without her.

Prepositions that take the genitive: Для — for; У — by, near; Без — without; Из — from, out of; От — away from. Я хочу́ пода́рок для моего́ дру́га — I want a present for my friend. Ко́фе без молока́ — Black coffee. Я из А́нглии — I'm from England.

Genitive adjectives: masculine and neuter -ого (-его for soft adjectives and after a hushing consonant), feminine -ой (-ей for soft adjectives and after a hushing consonant), plural -ых (-их): Кило́ хоро́шего ру́сского сы́ра — A kilogram of good Russian cheese. Кило́ хоро́шей ру́сской колбасы́ — A kilogram of good Russian sausage. Кило́ чи́стых све́жих я́блок — A kilogram of clean fresh apples. Я пришёл из моего старого дома — I arrived from my old house.

An animate plural direct object takes the genitive-shaped accusative: Эти женщины любят меня. — These women like me. Я люблю этих женщин. — I like these women.

references.title: The past tense
references.summary: Past-tense endings, agreement with the subject, and the past tense of the verb to be.
references.detail:
To form the past tense, remove -ть from the infinitive and add -л. Add -ла if the subject is feminine, -ло if it is neuter and -ли if it is plural.

The past tense agrees with its subject in gender and number, not in person. Он чита́л — He was reading. Она чита́ла — She was reading. Они чита́ли — They were reading.

The past forms of быть, to be, follow the regular pattern: бы́л for a masculine subject, была́ for a feminine subject, бы́ло for a neuter subject and бы́ли for a plural subject. Он был в Москве́ — He was in Moscow. Она была́ краси́вая — She was beautiful.

Some verbs, such as идти, have irregular past forms that cannot be predicted.

references.title: Reflexive verbs in the past
references.summary: How a reflexive verb keeps its reflexive ending in the past tense.
references.detail:
A reflexive verb such as улыба́ться, to smile, has a reflexive ending. To form its past tense, remove the reflexive ending, form the past tense, then reattach the ending: -ся after a consonant and -сь after a vowel.

Он улыба́лся — He was smiling. Она улыба́лась — She was smiling. Они улыба́лись — They were smiling.

The verb meaning to study follows the same pattern: учи́лся for a masculine subject, учи́лась for a feminine subject and учи́лись for a plural subject.

references.title: The future tense
references.summary: The compound future of imperfective verbs and the future of perfective verbs.
references.detail:
An imperfective verb forms its future with the future of быть and the infinitive: Я бу́ду говори́ть — I will be speaking. Мы бу́дем говори́ть — We will be speaking. Ты бу́дешь говори́ть — You will be speaking. Вы бу́дете говори́ть — You will be speaking. Он бу́дет говори́ть — He will be speaking.

A perfective verb's person forms have future meaning, with no separate future auxiliary: Я скажу́ — I will speak. Мы ска́жем — We will speak.

references.title: The dative singular and prepositional plural
references.summary: Dative singular nouns for the indirect object, and prepositional plural endings.
references.detail:
The dative case is traditionally the third grammatical case, and denotes the indirect object of a verb. кни́га — кни́ге. сто́л — столу́. до́м — до́му.

The prepositional plural ending is ах or ях. After a consonant the ending is ах. A noun ending in ь or й, in е or я, or with an irregular nominative plural ending in я, takes ях. кни́ги — кни́гах. столы́ — стола́х. дома́ — дома́х.

references.title: The five-letter spelling rule
references.summary: After ж, ц, ч, ш and щ, an unstressed o in an ending is written e.
references.detail: If the stem ends in ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, any unstressed o in an ending is instead written as e. For example, the good letter is written хорошее письмо, not хорошое письмо.

references.title: Aspect in the past
references.summary: Imperfective and perfective past forms of the verb meaning to read.
references.detail:
я читал — I was reading. я прочитал — I read. The imperfective presents an event as a process, or as a repeated or habitual event; the perfective presents it as a complete whole.

чита́л, чита́ла, чита́ло, чита́ли are the masculine, feminine, neuter and plural past forms of чита́ть. прочита́л, прочита́ла, прочита́ло are the masculine, feminine and neuter singular past forms of прочита́ть.

references.title: Reported speech
references.summary: Reporting a statement: English backshift and the Russian tense of the original.
references.detail:
In English, the reported verb usually changes tense after a past reporting verb, but this backshift is not mandatory in every report. Russian indirect speech generally keeps the tense of the original statement.

Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин reports “I am English” with no past copula. Я скажу ему ве́чером — I will tell him in the evening. Она́ сказа́ла, что она́ ска́жет ему́ ве́чером — She said that she would speak to him in the evening.

references.title: Aspect partners
references.summary: Two aspect pairs, learned as pairs.
references.detail: Each Russian verb is either perfective or imperfective, apart from a small number of verbs that are both. говори́ть is imperfective and сказа́ть is perfective. де́лать is imperfective and сде́лать is perfective. A prefix can make a perfective partner, but it can also make a verb with a new meaning, so learn each pair as a pair.

references.title: The future: person forms
references.summary: The compound future with быть and the future of a perfective verb, for every person.
references.detail:
The compound future puts a future form of быть before the imperfective infinitive, and the form of быть agrees with the subject. быть itself is an imperfective verb.

Я бу́ду говори́ть — I will be speaking. Мы бу́дем говори́ть — We will be speaking. Ты бу́дешь говори́ть — You will be speaking. Вы бу́дете говори́ть — You will be speaking. Он бу́дет говори́ть — He will be speaking. Они бу́дут говори́ть — They will be speaking.

A perfective verb forms its future by conjugating it, with no separate future auxiliary. Я скажу́ — I will speak. Мы ска́жем — We will speak. Ты ска́жешь — You will speak. Вы ска́жете — You will speak. Он ска́жет — He will speak. Они ска́жут — They will speak.

references.title: Aspect in the future
references.summary: A limited stretch of an activity, and the compound future without a stated limit.
references.detail: Я порабо́таю три ча́са — I will work for three hours. Я бу́ду рабо́тать — I will work. A stated duration does not by itself require perfective aspect. Russian also has verbs that present an activity for a limited stretch, which is different from doing it to completion.

references.title: Impersonal states in the past
references.summary: Cold and bored states with the person in the dative.
references.detail: For the cold and bored states shown here, the person is in the dative, and the past tense uses было in the neuter singular. Ему было холодно — He was cold. Им было скучно — They were bored. ей было холодно — she was cold.

In this course a stress mark over a vowel shows the stressed vowel; the mark is a reading aid that ordinary print leaves out. за́мок, stressed on the first vowel, means castle, and замо́к, stressed on the second vowel, means lock. му́ка means torment and мука́ means flour. steps.title: Different letters, same final sound
steps.body: At the end of a word said on its own, a voiced consonant letter is pronounced like its voiceless partner: г like к, д like т. steps.title: Review the three groups
steps.body:
So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. Learn each word with its group; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. учи́тель — teacher. друг — friend is also masculine. Learn the group with each word; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. ма́ма — mom. дверь — door is feminine too. Learn the group with each word; do not guess the group of another word from its ending.

These words are neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea. 

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

steps.title: Identify the noun’s case role
steps.body: In the supplied Муж говорит, the husband is the subject and the talking verb states its action. The noun names the subject, in the nominative case. steps.title: Separate the subject from its description
steps.body: In Поезд старый, the train is the subject noun and old is its predicate description. This present property clause has no overt Russian copula. The noun’s case role is nominative subject, not accusative direct object. A dictionary-looking noun or familiar translation alone does not identify its role in every construction.

steps.title: Apply the distinction to a different supplied noun
steps.body: Студент новый supplies a second independent property clause: the student is the subject noun, and new describes that subject. Its case role is nominative subject. Keep Муж говорит — The husband is talking and Поезд старый — The train is old as correct sentence meanings. Other constructions have nominative predicate nouns; not every nominative noun is a subject.

sessions.title: Possessives that agree with the noun

steps.title: My: agreement with the noun
steps.body: In мой стол, the noun стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, the noun собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

steps.title: Match gender, number and case
steps.body: Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

steps.title: Our: a worked case change
steps.body: Наш means our; Ваш means your (formal or plural). на́ша is the feminine singular nominative form of наш, and сестра́ is a feminine singular noun. In the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша becomes на́шу, and сестра́ becomes сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего is the masculine and neuter genitive form, and на́ши is plural.

steps.title: Masculine and feminine forms
steps.body: In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

steps.title: Neuter and plural forms
steps.body: моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form.

steps.title: Your: masculine and feminine
steps.body: тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the form that matches the noun. Then read why the other forms do not fit.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form.

sessions.title: Adjective endings that agree with the noun

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: новый карандаш is masculine singular nominative; новая машина is feminine singular nominative. The adjective agrees with the noun in the phrase, so the car phrase uses the feminine form но́вая rather than masculine но́вый or plural но́вые. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective но́вая becomes но́вую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Both words change in these supplied case pairs. In Анна встретила новую учительницу (Anna met the new teacher), the adjective новую and the noun учительницу are both accusative.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: The dictionary form of this adjective is masculine singular nominative но́вый. A phrase can need another gender, number or case even though the dictionary form is masculine singular nominative. In the neuter, the adjective но́вое becomes но́вого in the genitive, and the noun окно́ becomes окна́. Both adjective and noun change case while remaining neuter singular. In Я пришёл из моего старого дома (I arrived from my old house), the words моего старого дома are all genitive.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: новое платье is neuter singular nominative. Compare the adjective with the masculine pencil and feminine car examples above: the noun controls the agreement required in that phrase. синий стол uses the masculine nominative form of a different adjective meaning dark blue. Learn the forms of each adjective as you meet them.

steps.title: One adjective, several forms
steps.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

steps.title: Two spelling conditions
steps.body: After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

steps.title: Gender and a worked case change
steps.body: хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective хоро́шая becomes хоро́шую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Keep the same noun when you change the case. хоро́шего is masculine singular genitive; хоро́шие is plural nominative. In Оно́ под хоро́шими кни́гами (It's under the good books), the adjective хоро́шими and the noun кни́гами are both instrumental plural.

steps.title: Singular, plural and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший.

sessions.title: Recognize nominative forms and plural spelling

steps.title: Singular and plural forms
steps.body: Adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. This lesson compares singular and plural nominative forms, then explains the spelling in the plurals.

steps.title: The seven-letter spelling rule
steps.body: After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, or щ, write и rather than ы. The seven-letter condition is required. This rule applies to the spelling of noun and adjective endings. In кни́ги, и follows г; in хоро́шие, и follows ш. Read the form carefully before answering.

steps.title: A worked noun plural
steps.body: кни́га means book in the singular, and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. The stem ends in г, so the seven-letter rule requires и. In the other direction, кни́ги becomes кни́га in the singular nominative.

steps.title: Two plural forms, different patterns
steps.body: кни́ги is plural nominative in this lesson. дни is also plural nominative and means days. Its и does not follow a letter in the seven-letter set, so дни is not an example of that spelling replacement. Not every plural ending in и comes from the seven-letter rule. Identify number from the form and its context.

steps.title: Adjective number and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative; хоро́шие is plural nominative. The neuter singular form хоро́шее becomes хоро́шие in the plural nominative, and хоро́шие becomes хоро́шее in the neuter singular. The masculine singular dictionary form is хоро́ший. Choose the form with the specified grammatical features.

steps.title: Choose one by gender
steps.body: один мальчик — one boy; одна девушка — one girl. For these singular counting examples, one agrees with the noun: masculine один and feminine одна. Both still mean one.

steps.title: Choose the form of two
steps.body: два is the form for masculine and neuter counted nouns; две is the feminine form. The supplied example две девушки — two girls uses feminine две. The following noun is genitive singular in this counting construction; the numeral choice still follows its gender.

steps.title: Recognize neuter and plural-form one
steps.body: одно животное — one animal uses neuter singular одно. одни джинсы — one [pair of] jeans uses plural одни with the plural-form noun. The plural numeral here does not mean several pairs; these are different gender/number forms of one.

steps.title: Keep the value while changing agreement
steps.body: одна́ and одно́ both represent 1. They are feminine and neuter singular forms, respectively.

steps.title: Distinguish plural one from feminine two
steps.body: одни́ represents 1 in the supplied plural-form example, while две represents 2 with a feminine noun. Distinguish одни джинсы from две девушки by the complete supplied construction, rather than treating every plural-looking form as two.

steps.title: Apply masculine one to a different noun
steps.body: оди́н — one and два — two. The additional example один час uses masculine singular один with час; feminine singular одна is the form shown with девушка.

steps.title: Start with the construction
steps.body: These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. A count ending in one outside the teen exception uses a nominative singular noun in the shown basic phrases. один час — one hour. два часа — two hours.

steps.title: Two, three and four
steps.body: A count ending in two, three or four outside the teen exception uses a genitive singular noun in the basic construction. This is a grammatical singular form even though the count is greater than one.

steps.title: Genitive plural counts
steps.body: Counts ending in zero or five through nine use genitive plural in the basic construction. The teen exception also uses genitive plural. Ten and sixteen therefore fit this pattern. пять часов — five hours. двадцать один час — twenty-one hours.

steps.title: Compound counts
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare 21 and 22: their final digits select different noun cases; being larger than five is not enough to choose genitive plural. двадцать два часа — twenty-two hours. две девушки — two girls.

steps.title: Teen values and exceptions
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. All counts from 11 through19 use genitive plural here. For 15 through19 the final digit already leads to genitive plural;11 through14 override the one/two/three/four ending pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles.

steps.title: One and zero endings
steps.body: The example with 41 follows the final-one pattern and uses nominative singular for the counted noun. The example with 10 follows the zero-ending pattern and uses genitive plural. десять копеек — ten kopeks. сорок один год — forty-one years.

steps.title: Hundreds preserve the boundary
steps.body: The count 203 ends in 03, so final three selects genitive singular in the basic counting phrase. The count 213 ends in 13, so the teen exception selects genitive plural. пять лет — five years. двести три собаки — two hundred and three dogs.

steps.title: Possession and the genitive
steps.body: This unit covers possession and absence, the genitive forms of pronouns, nouns and adjectives after prepositions, and animate plural objects.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 10 in the copy you own.

steps.title: The possessor and the possessed thing
steps.body: In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son?

steps.title: Possession versus absence
steps.body: A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

steps.title: Positive statements and questions
steps.body: The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend.

steps.title: Keep quantity and absence separate
steps.body: The many-friends example includes a quantity expression. Quantity patterns are separate from the simple nominative possessed thing. The no-son example below denies possession and uses the genitive for the absent thing. У моего нового мужа есть много друзе́й — My new husband has many friends. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son.

steps.title: Another absence example
steps.body: The no-money example also denies possession. Choose the genitive absence explanation, rather than the simple positive possession explanation. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

steps.title: Identify absence
steps.body: In an absence line, the absent thing is genitive. An absence line may describe what a person does not have or what does not exist at a place. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son. Нет рестора́нов — There are no restaurants.

steps.title: Choose a complete case explanation
steps.body: The absence construction uses a genitive noun for the absent thing. The simple positive possession construction instead uses a genitive possessor and a nominative possessed thing. Choose from the meaning and construction of the whole supplied line.

steps.title: Apply the absence pattern
steps.body: Both negative examples below use the genitive for the absent thing. Keep the absent thing separate from any possessor or place mentioned in the line. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

steps.body: The positive son example below affirms possession. Its possessed noun is nominative, so the genitive absence explanation does not classify this line. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son.

steps.title: Aspect and time
steps.body: Aspect describes how an action is viewed, not when it happens. Imperfective can present an action as a process or as a repeated or habitual event. Perfective presents an event with its boundary or result. Imperfective does not by itself mean unfinished. говори́ть is imperfective; сказа́ть is perfective. Learn the two supplied infinitives.

steps.title: The saying and telling pair
steps.body: Many Russian verbs are learned in an aspect pair, but not every verb has two words, and a pair is not automatic. говорить and сказать are context-dependent counterparts, not a universal pair for the English verb speak. For the saying/telling pair shown here, the perfective counterpart of говори́ть is сказа́ть; the imperfective counterpart of сказа́ть is говори́ть.

steps.title: A worked doing and making pair
steps.body: де́лать is imperfective; сде́лать is perfective. Both concern doing or making. The perfective presents the action as a complete whole; the imperfective presents it as a process. говори́ть concerns speaking or saying and belongs to the other pair. Learn the shown pair rather than assuming every prefix changes only aspect.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the counterpart from the saying/telling pair. Then compare its aspect and meaning with the other option.

steps.title: One noun, different cases
steps.body: The instrumental case can mark the means used to do something. These checks first teach its forms. сто́л is the dictionary form, meaning table; столо́м is instrumental singular. The word still names a table: the ending marks its grammatical role, not a new vocabulary meaning.

steps.title: A bounded noun ending
steps.body: The instrumental singular -ом fits the hard stem of the relevant noun class. Soft stems use their own instrumental ending, so -ом is not universal. Here, keep the stem of сто́л and add -ом to obtain столо́м. Learn the stress with the whole form.

steps.title: Compare the other cases
steps.body: столу́ is dative singular and столе́ is prepositional singular. Both belong to the same noun, but neither has the instrumental singular ending. For an instrumental singular request, select столо́м rather than selecting a form merely because its English gloss is table.

steps.title: Work the house form
steps.body: до́м means house in its dictionary form. до́мом is instrumental singular: keep the stem and add -ом. Given до́м and an instrumental singular request, choose до́мом. This is the same ending pattern as the table form.

steps.title: Check case before choosing
steps.body: до́му is dative singular; до́ме is prepositional singular. They do not answer an instrumental singular request. Compare the entire ending with до́мом, and notice that this noun keeps its stem stress.

steps.title: Meaning and form together
steps.body: поездом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning train; карандашом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning pencil. The pencil check asks for that meaning as well as the case. Its other options refer to train and husband. A correct case alone does not identify the requested noun.

steps.title: A different singular pattern
steps.body: книгой is the instrumental singular form for book. This noun has a different ending from the -ом shown for table and house. Do not attach the same ending to every noun. These examples introduce selected singular patterns, not the full instrumental paradigm.

steps.title: Instrumental plural of book
steps.body: Instrumental plural refers to more than one. кни́га is the dictionary singular form for book; кни́гами is instrumental plural. Keep the stem and use -ами in this pattern. Given an instrumental plural request, choose кни́гами.

steps.title: Plural noun endings
steps.body: Instrumental plural nouns commonly use -ами or -ями, with exceptions. The book, house and table forms shown here use -ами. This is a noun ending; adjectives have their own agreement endings. These checks ask you to recognize the displayed pattern, not derive every noun form.

steps.title: Compare plural cases
steps.body: кни́гам is dative plural; кни́гах is prepositional plural. Neither is instrumental plural. Compare their endings with кни́гами: the final vowel is part of the instrumental plural ending here.

steps.title: Work the house plural
steps.body: до́м names a house in the dictionary singular. дома́ми is instrumental plural. For this plural case request choose дома́ми, including the stress shown in the retained form.

steps.title: Case and number both matter
steps.body: дома́м is dative plural. до́мом is instrumental singular. The first has the wrong case; the second has the right case but the wrong number for an instrumental plural request. дома́ми meets both requirements.

steps.title: Work the table plural

steps.title: Reject a singular instrumental
steps.body: стола́м is dative plural; столо́м is instrumental singular. Neither meets both parts of an instrumental plural request. стола́ми supplies instrumental case and plural number together.

steps.title: Adjective agreement
steps.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in case and number, and in gender in the singular. хоро́ший is the masculine dictionary form for good. хоро́шим is its masculine or neuter instrumental singular form. Here the check requests masculine instrumental; it does not ask for an English gloss.

steps.title: Adjective endings differ
steps.body: Hard-stem masculine and neuter adjectives take -ым in the instrumental, and the soft or spelling-restricted stems take -им. These are adjective declension endings. хоро́шим uses -им because of the spelling restriction after its stem-final consonant. Do not apply the noun ending -ом to this adjective.

steps.title: Compare dative and plural
steps.body: хоро́шему is dative masculine or neuter singular. хоро́шие is nominative plural. Neither is the masculine instrumental singular form requested here. Work the choice by selecting хоро́шим.

steps.title: Instrumental plural agreement
steps.body: хоро́шими is instrumental plural, with a plural adjective ending. хоро́шая is feminine nominative singular. For a plural instrumental request select хоро́шими; хоро́шим has singular number. Recognizing these forms does not by itself demonstrate using adjective agreement in a sentence.

steps.title: Two meanings of with
steps.body: Я написал хорошим новым карандашом — I wrote with a good new pencil. The pencil is the tool used for writing: this is the means instrumental, without a preposition before the tool phrase. Я хочу встречу с интересной русской женщиной — I want a meeting with an interesting Russian woman. Here with introduces the person involved in the meeting: this is the accompaniment line, using a preposition followed by instrumental forms.

steps.title: Work the role contrast
steps.body: For a means instrumental request, choose the writing sentence because its pencil is the instrument. For an accompaniment line request, choose the meeting sentence because it describes being with a person. English with can express both roles; its presence alone does not decide which Russian construction is used. Read what the phrase contributes to the event.

steps.title: A separate spatial role
steps.body: Я живу́ ме́жду двумя но́выми дома́ми — I live between two new houses. This is the between line: the phrase locates the speaker relative to two houses. The houses are neither a writing tool nor a companion. Work the choice by identifying location rather than treating every instrumental phrase as a means phrase.

steps.title: Above and below
steps.body: над — over. под — under. These spatial meanings contrast vertical positions. The over label belongs to the first preposition; the under label belongs to the second. In a location construction, both can govern instrumental forms. The questions here recognize meanings from isolated prepositions; they do not ask you to choose a noun ending.

steps.title: Case depends on the construction
steps.body: The same preposition can govern different cases in different uses. For the preposition meaning under, instrumental describes location, while accusative can describe a destination under something. Movement within a location does not by itself require accusative: distinguish where something is from where it is going. These isolated-word checks contain no movement context and therefore do not assess that case choice.

steps.title: Before and between

Between places something relative to two things. When choosing a displayed English label, compare the specific spatial meaning, including the alternative behind. Learn the meaning first; sentence use still requires the appropriate case.

sessions.title: Recognize verbs used with instrumental complements

steps.title: Becoming and remaining
steps.body: стать means to become. остаться means to remain. Both are infinitives: they name an action or state without marking a past event. Becoming expresses a change; remaining expresses continuation. For the first form choose to become. For the second form choose remain among the displayed choices. The English past-tense word became does not correctly label either infinitive.

steps.title: What a complement describes
steps.body: An instrumental complement can describe the role or state of the subject after a linking verb, rather than an instrument used to carry out an action. The verbs shown in this lesson can occur in that construction. These checks show only the verbs and ask for their meanings. Recognizing a verb meaning is a first step; it does not demonstrate forming a complete sentence with an instrumental complement.

steps.title: Appearance and discovery
steps.body: казаться — appear to be. оказаться — turn out to be. The first concerns how something seems; the second concerns what it proves to be. Work the second choice by selecting turn out to be, rather than the meaning of continuation. A displayed infinitive still does not specify a past event. Keep these meanings distinct from becoming and remaining.

steps.body: Compare the meanings and roles explained above, then choose from the displayed alternatives. A missed check returns to all explanations and examples.

steps.title: Position rather than quantity
steps.body: пе́рвый — first. второ́й — second. тре́тий — third. четвёртый — fourth. An ordinal identifies position in an ordered sequence; a cardinal tells how many. These isolated ordinal forms are masculine nominative singular. Learn the position expressed by each form before choosing it.

steps.title: Ordinals agree like adjectives
steps.body: Ordinals agree with their noun in gender, number and case, like adjectives. восемнадцатую девушку means the eighteenth girl as a feminine accusative noun phrase. The retained example comes from a sentence about photographing her; this displayed fragment alone does not mean She just photographed. The ordinal ending follows the noun phrase, rather than staying in the masculine dictionary form. These recognition checks do not assess producing agreement in a sentence.

steps.title: Work the requested position
steps.body: For the first ordinal, choose пе́рвый; for the second ordinal, choose второ́й; for the third ordinal, choose тре́тий. четвёртый expresses fourth, so it fails each of those requests. Read the English request: the separately shown Russian cue may name a different position and is not the target to copy.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Read the requested position or quantity and compare the forms explained above, then choose from the displayed alternatives. A missed check returns to all explanations and examples.

sessions.title: Distinguish the supplied clock-time and object-selection questions

steps.title: Understand the whole question
steps.body: Который час? — What time is it? This fixed question asks for the current clock time. The noun час normally means hour; its retained example label time reflects this question context rather than a universal translation of the isolated noun. Learn the complete question as a unit.

steps.title: Read the full question and the requested information
steps.body: Forms of который do not by themselves identify a clock question. Read the complete supplied question and its noun. Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. This is the guided ownership/selection example. Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? Asks which book the listener wants. The listener is asked to choose a book. Который час? — What time is it? Asks for the current clock time. This requests the current clock time, not which book the listener wants or which apple belongs to the speaker. The independent clock and book cues are different complete questions from the guided apple cue. These checks recognize the supplied meanings; they do not demonstrate independently asking/giving a new time or forming every interrogative. Optional repeated clock gloss practice is separate from the required checks.

sessions.title: Interpret quarter, half and time remaining

steps.title: A quarter into the next named hour
steps.body: четверть восьмого — 7:15. The eighth hour is the period leading up to eight, not the period starting at eight. A quarter of that hour has elapsed after seven. The ordinal names the next hour and appears in genitive form.

steps.title: Half of the hour in progress
steps.body: полвосьмого — 7:30. Half of the eighth hour has passed, so the clock shows half past seven. The compact half-hour expression is written as one word in this retained form. Match the construction to the clock reading, rather than treating the named eighth hour as the elapsed whole hour.

steps.title: A quarter remaining before eight
steps.body: без четверти восемь — 7:45. This construction counts a quarter hour remaining until eight: subtract fifteen minutes from the named upcoming hour. The without construction differs from counting a quarter or a half already elapsed. These choices interpret existing forms; context is still needed to distinguish morning from evening.

steps.title: Clock readings and event times
steps.body: A current-time question and the time when an event happens are different requests. The retained event sentences use at-time expressions. A preposition introduces several of them, while the without construction expresses minutes remaining until the upcoming hour. Study the complete source examples before selecting their readings.

steps.title: On the hour and contextual AM or PM

The bare six-hour and one-hour expressions do not themselves distinguish evening from morning; the source readings depend on context. Do not infer that every occurrence of six means eighteen.

steps.title: Quarter past and the next ordinal
steps.body: Я приду в четверть восьмого. — 7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour. Он нам позвонил в пятнадцать минут десятого. — 9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour. A quarter or fifteen minutes has elapsed in the hour leading to the named next hour. The ordinal is genitive; the event-time phrase also has its introductory preposition.

steps.title: Half past in two retained constructions
steps.body: Наш рейс уезжает в половине пятого. — 4.30 – half of the fifth hour. Мы будем свободны в полвторого. — 1.30 – half of the second hour. Both name a half elapsed in the next ordinal hour. Their retained preposition and noun forms differ; recognize each complete construction rather than exchanging endings mechanically.

Subtract the stated remaining minutes from the upcoming hour. The preposition meaning without governs the remaining quantity in genitive form. These existing choices do not assess independently building a new event-time sentence.

steps.title: Comparing a quality
steps.body: бо́льший — bigger. лу́чший — better. These retained forms concern degree of a quality, rather than naming an unrelated object. The first compares size. The second is the source gloss used by the existing choice; it can mean best in context, so better here is not a universal translation. These full adjective forms can change for gender, number and case; they are not the same construction as an unchanging short comparative. Qualified review of the contextual gloss remains pending.

steps.title: One-word and two-word comparisons
steps.body: красне́е — redder. бо́лее до́брый — kinder. The first is a short comparative with an ending expressing a higher degree of redness; this short form does not change for gender, number or case. The second combines a word meaning more with the ordinary long adjective meaning kind. In this two-word construction the adjective still changes for agreement. Not every adjective has a one-word comparative, and these examples do not give a complete formation rule for unfamiliar adjectives.

steps.title: Comparative versus superlative
steps.body: наибо́льший — the biggest. This retained superlative identifies the greatest size in the relevant group, rather than just a greater degree. Contrast the source labels бо́лее — more, ме́нее — less, and наиме́нее — least. More and less express comparison; least identifies the lowest degree. For наибо́льший select the biggest, not more or less. For бо́лее до́брый select kinder, not least or bigger. These choices recognize existing forms; they do not assess independently forming new comparisons or a complete comparison sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish which questions from relative clauses

steps.title: Questions selecting an apple or a book
steps.body: Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? These are direct questions asking which member is selected, not relative clauses modifying an earlier noun. In the apple question the selecting form agrees with a neuter singular subject in the nominative. In the book question it agrees with a feminine singular direct object in the accusative. Match the whole question: ownership of an apple differs from wanting a book.

steps.title: A relative clause adds information about a noun
steps.body: Человек, который изменил мир — The man who changed the world. The clause following the comma describes the preceding person; it does not ask which person. The relative form takes masculine singular agreement from that noun, and nominative case because it is the subject of changed inside its own clause. For a relative form, gender and number come from the noun it describes; case comes from the role inside the relative clause, not automatically from the preceding noun.

steps.title: With whom: a preposition inside the relative clause
steps.body: Же́нщина, с кото́рой я дружу́ — The woman (who) I'm friends with. The relative clause describes the woman. Its relative form has feminine singular agreement and instrumental case after the preposition meaning with. Russian keeps this preposition before the relative form, while the retained English rendering places with at the end. Compare the woman described by friendship with the man described by changing the world and the two direct questions. Recognizing these meanings does not demonstrate independently choosing a relative case or producing a new clause.

sessions.title: Distinguish changed meanings and genuine aspect partners

steps.title: Different prefixes can change the meaning
steps.body: отговорить — to dissuade. договориться — to agree. These are different meanings, even though the words share material with a verb of speaking. A prefix is not always just an aspect marker: learn the whole verb and its meaning.

steps.title: The actual dissuade aspect pair
steps.body: отговаривать is the imperfective partner of perfective отговорить: both concern dissuading. The retained source explicitly identifies this pair. сказать belongs to a separate speaking pair; it is not the imperfective partner of отговорить. For a question asking for the perfective partner of отговаривать, select отговорить. договориться is a different verb meaning to agree.

steps.title: Keep the other meanings separate
steps.body: написать — to write. сделать — to do. Neither expresses dissuading or agreeing. When a question asks for a meaning, translate the displayed verb. When it asks for an aspect partner, preserve the lexical meaning while changing aspect. These selections do not demonstrate creating new prefixed verbs or using aspect in a sentence.

sessions.title: Interpret conditional structure and speaker agreement

steps.title: The past form with a conditional particle
steps.body: я спал бы is used by a male speaker; я спала́ бы is used by a female speaker. These labels describe the speaker marked by the past-form agreement; they are not translations of the whole expressions. Both use the first-person pronoun, a past-form verb and the conditional particle. In this construction the past form need not report an actual past event: it can express a hypothetical situation, such as I would sleep. Context supplies the time reference.

steps.title: Read agreement rather than an English sentence label
steps.body: Compare the two retained forms я спал бы and я спала́ бы. The feminine past form has a final vowel that the masculine form lacks. For the first choose a male speaker; for the second choose a female speaker. I would like to sleep is a sentence meaning, not a label identifying the gender marked by the shown past form. Speaker agreement and sentence meaning are different questions.

steps.title: A wish and a different position for the particle
steps.body: я бы поспа́л — I would like to sleep. я бы поспала́ has feminine speaker agreement: the speaker is marked feminine. The first-person pronoun identifies the speaker, rather than another person. These retained wish expressions have the conditional particle before the verb, whereas the earlier examples put it after the verb. It cannot begin its clause. The wish reading comes from the construction and context, not from translating every conditional particle as would like. These choices do not demonstrate independently forming a conditional sentence or an aspect choice.

steps.body: я должен — I have to. This retained phrase expresses obligation for a masculine singular speaker. steps.body: должна — If the subject is feminine. должно — If the subject is neuter. должны — If the subject is plural. steps.title: An expected eclipse
steps.body: Затме́ние должно́ наступи́ть в три часа́. — The eclipse should occur at three o'clock. Here should expresses an expected event, not a duty imposed on the eclipse. The short adjective agrees with the neuter subject and the infinitive names the event. The retained usage description is (with a verb) Used to express likelihood. Usually translated as "should".

steps.title: An employee obligation

The English label an obligation describes a required action; an expected event describes a prediction such as the eclipse. Context determines which sense the shared adjective-plus-infinitive structure expresses. One independent check asks for the eclipse sentence meaning; the other classifies the employee obligation. These two examples do not demonstrate independent sentence production or every use of the adjective.

objectives.title: Distinguish motion meaning, directionality and setting out

steps.title: Admitted motion lines
steps.body: Proposed Unit 20 uses admitted motion lines for direction, foot and transport, carrying and leading, setting out, and selected prefixed paths. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 20 in the copy you own.

sessions.title: Distinguish motion meaning, directionality and setting out

steps.title: Walking and travelling by vehicle
steps.body: идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

steps.title: Directionality is separate from aspect
steps.body: The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

steps.title: Carrying, leading and transporting
steps.body: нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

steps.title: Setting out does not assert arrival
steps.body: Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

steps.title: Read the path and only the displayed clause
steps.body: Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они улетят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

steps.title: Interpret directionality in a whole example
steps.body: Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

steps.title: Distinguish repeated trips and a completed return
steps.body: Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the retained supplied context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). The past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. A choice saying “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” makes an incorrect aspect inference for these forms. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.

There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они улетят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the retained supplied context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). The past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. A choice saying “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” makes an incorrect aspect inference for these forms. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.

sessions.title: Connect own possession to the subject and the possessed noun

steps.title: Who owns it and which noun controls the form
steps.body: The reflexive possessive refers to the subject as the owner. Its gender, number and case agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner. The retained dictionary forms are свой, своя, своё and свои. A masculine owner and a feminine owner can therefore use the same possessive form with the same noun.

steps.title: The movie belongs to the subject
steps.body: Бо́ря рассказа́л о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Borya told about his favorite movie.). А́нна рассказа́ла о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Anna told about her favorite movie.). In each sentence the favorite movie belongs to the subject. The movie noun has the same gender, number and case in both, so the possessive form stays the same. The name and past-verb agreement change. The exercise asks you to preserve that movie object while changing the subject.

steps.title: The same own book with two subjects
steps.body: Свое́й кни́ги она́ никогда́ не написа́ла. — (She never wrote her own book.). Свое́й кни́ги он никогда́ не написа́л. — (He never wrote his own book.). The possessive agrees with the feminine singular book noun; the shown form is genitive in this negative sentence. Changing the subject changes the past verb's agreement, not the book phrase. These sentences are about a book, not a movie or jeans.

steps.title: Plural jeans and the limits of the checks
steps.body: Бо́ря наде́л свои́ джи́нсы. — (Borya put on his own jeans.). А́нна наде́ла свои́ джи́нсы. — (Anna put on her own jeans.). Plural jeans require plural possessive agreement regardless of whether Borya or Anna owns them. The exercise keeps this object and changes the subject. The checks select supplied matched sentences; they do not demonstrate independently declining the possessive or constructing an ownership sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish oneself from a possessed object

steps.title: The person loved and the person who owns
steps.body: Я люблю́ себя́ — I love myself. Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ — I love my wife. In the first sentence the object refers back to the subject. In the second the object is a wife; the parenthesized possessive makes ownership explicit. Loving oneself and loving a wife describe different objects.

steps.title: A whole sentence is more than its object word
steps.body: жену́ is the accusative form of the noun meaning wife. It does not mean I love. In Я люблю́ свою́ жену́ the verb supplies loving and the noun supplies its object. The full displayed sentence Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ means I love my wife; the full displayed sentence Я люблю́ себя́ means I love myself. Choose the whole-sentence meaning rather than translating the object word as the verb. These checks recognize the supplied love and wounded-object sentences; they do not demonstrate independently choosing every reflexive case form.

steps.title: Recognize the same-person object in a different sentence
steps.body: Он поранил себя — He has wounded himself. Here the subject denotes the man and the direct object себя refers back to that same person. The verb and subject differ from guided Я люблю́ себя́. Compare the complete supplied Он поранил его — He has wounded him (someone else). In this contrast the other person is the object; the person wounded is different from the subject. In both wounded sentences the object is a person, not a possessed wife. In the retained Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ example, a wife is the object even when the possessive refers to the subject as owner. Keep object identity separate from ownership. These are supplied direct-object readings, not productive grammar, every pronoun case, emphasis or a rule that the reflexive-verb suffix always means accidental action.

sessions.title: Distinguish purpose, condition, cause and concession

steps.title: Purpose and condition
steps.body: чтобы — so that. если — if. The first conjunction can introduce a purpose; the second introduces a condition. In a purpose construction with the same subject for both actions, an infinitive after the purpose conjunction can name the intended action. This rule is explained here, but the current choices do not require composing such a sentence.

steps.title: Ordinary purpose wording
steps.body: чтобы is an ordinary purpose conjunction. The bookish or archaic qualifier in the retained source belongs to дабы, not to чтобы. The English meaning so that differs from the conditional if and the causal because. Select the meaning of the displayed conjunction; do not infer an archaic register for the ordinary form.

steps.title: Cause, concession and time
steps.body: потому что — because. хотя — although. The first gives a reason; the second introduces a concession. The English label after names a temporal relationship rather than a reason. English since can also express a reason, so it is not a contrasting wrong answer to because in this exercise. The causal check instead contrasts because with although and after. These conjunction meanings are distinct from purpose and condition.
