An active participle describes an entity performing the action. The retained чита́вшая is the past reading form; чита́ющая is the present reading form. The labels in the past and in the present distinguish these supplied forms. They do not identify a passive entity being read. An English description of reading can express the action without itself specifying this past/present contrast.

For чита́ющая, select in the present when asked for its time label. For чита́вшая, select in the past for its own time label. One retained contrast check instead asks for the other time: there the answer is in the present. That reversed question does not turn the displayed past form into a present form. The gloss that read names an action; it is not the requested contrasting time label.

The retained живу́щие has the meaning living and illustrates an active description. This is recognition of the admitted example, not a general algorithm for generating participles of unfamiliar verbs. Interpreting an isolated form does not establish the complete tense or actor of a sentence that has not been supplied.

Contrast the adverbial opening with finite coordination

provenanceRecords.shippedText: In Закончив письмо, Анна пошла на почту., finishing the letter is expressed by the opening verbal adverb. In Анна закончила письмо и пошла на почту., the actions are expressed by coordinated finite verbs. The adverbial opening is the bookish option and the finite coordination the ordinary option in this admitted pair. Both describe finishing before going to the post office; the register choice does not reverse those events.

provenanceRecords.shippedText: The supplied отправила его means she sent it, with the letter as the object in this passage. The passage places the sending after Anna goes to the post office. It does not say that she stayed at the table, finished at the market, left the letter at home or received a letter at home. Those alternatives replace a stated event or location. Bookish register classification is a separate objective and cannot answer who acted, where she went or what she did with the letter.

In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? 

A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend.

The absence construction uses a genitive noun for the absent thing. The simple positive possession construction instead uses a genitive possessor and a nominative possessed thing. Choose from the meaning and construction of the whole supplied line.

Both negative examples below use the genitive for the absent thing. Keep the absent thing separate from any possessor or place mentioned in the line. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money. 

The positive son example below affirms possession. Its possessed noun is nominative, so the genitive absence explanation does not classify this line. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son.

These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. In these basic examples, a final one outside the teen exception uses nominative singular; final two, three or four use genitive singular. один час — один час. три кошки — three cats. 

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. All teen counts in the supplied basic examples take genitive plural.

Five and sixteen both use genitive plural in these counting examples. The complete value matters: a compound count ending in one outside the teen exception has a different pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles. 

The I saw two friends sentence has an animate accusative object. Both the numeral and noun are declined; do not classify it with the basic nominative/inanimate accusative rule. The one-cat example below instead states existence in the basic nominative context. Я видел двух друзей — I saw two friends. Есть оди́н кот — There is one cat.

Both are past forms. English simple past wording alone does not determine Russian aspect; the question explicitly asks for the perfective form.

A completed activity can still be described with imperfective aspect when the focus is on the process; English simple past can also translate an imperfective verb.

The grammatical check asks which form is shown, rather than its English gloss. Long adjectives have case, gender and number inflection; short adjectives vary for gender and number, not case. The retained examples are recognition targets, not a universal rule for producing short forms by removing endings.

In the taught modern use, short adjectives occur only in the nominative and are used predicatively to describe their subject. A long adjective often describes a noun attributively and can also be a predicate. The choice depends on the sentence, not a universal rule about one fixed word position. The isolated pair does not provide a complete context for selecting every long-versus-short form; broader agreement and sentence-level application remain pending.

The retained беж means beige and is an invariant colour form, unchanged for case, gender and number. Its short appearance does not make it the short counterpart of но́вый. Keep lexical meaning, inflection and adjective function separate. The correct glosses remain in Vocabulary Lab as word-meaning practice; they do not satisfy the independent adjective grammar checks.

A long adjective can modify a noun attributively and can also be a predicate. The choice depends on the sentence, not a universal rule about one fixed word position. CC BY-SA4.0 through retained Wikipedia:Copyrights oldid1369466282 and existing source/rights declarations. The source states unprefixed pairs are imperfective. One-direction motion in progress, ability/general motion, movement in various directions, repeated trips and a past completed round trip are distinct supplied uses. Completion of a round trip does not turn the unprefixed form into a perfective. Prefixed setting-out/path meanings remain separately taught and are not inferred from these labels. Native clauses and bilingual notes are direct selections unchanged; no generated sentence, punctuation deletion, stress insertion or private Penguin text. All earlier lexical/prefixed checks and guided classification remain preserved. идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они улетят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the retained supplied context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). The past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. A choice saying “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” makes an incorrect aspect inference for these forms. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.

идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они улетят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

A perfective verbal adverb normally presents an action completed before the main action in this taught construction. Anterior means earlier relative to that action. The retained сказав and научившись illustrate these forms; their labels alone do not fix an absolute past tense. Read the accompanying main predicate to establish the sentence time.

In написав письмо, она отправит его завтра, she will send the letter tomorrow after writing it. The writing precedes the future sending: anterior to a future main action is the matching description. The sentence does not require the writing to have happened before the present moment. The pronoun she names the main subject, and the writer and sender are the same person. An absolute present label loses the relative timing; assigning a different subject loses the supplied construction.

The retained войдя illustrates another perfective verbal-adverb form with an action normally anterior to its main predicate. It does not by itself identify a main subject or an absolute sentence tense. Compare the supplied forms and read their complete contexts when available. This small example set supplies recognition practice, not a complete productive algorithm for unlisted verbs.

==Nouns== The accusative case is a peculiar case in Russian, as it makes a distinction that other cases do not. Specifically, if a masculine word denotes an inanimate thing ('table', 'chair', etc), then it remains the same as the nominative. If, however, a masculine word denotes a person or animal ('man', 'son', 'cow', etc), then the case uses the endings of the [[Russian/Grammar/Genitive case|''genitive case'']]. For plurals in the accusative, no matter what gender the word, they are also split: any plural word that's inanimate is identical to its [[Russian/Grammar/Nominative case|nominative plural form]], while animate plural words follow the rules for the genitive plural. Some examples highlighting this distinction are as follows: :* This chair is brown. - '''Этот ''стул'' коричневый.''' - Nominative of an inanimate noun :*I made a chair. - '''Я де́лал ''стул.''''' - Accusative of the noun :*This cat likes me. - '''''Этот кот'' любит меня.''' - Nom. of an animate noun :*I like this cat. - '''Я люблю ''этого кота.''''' - Acc. of the noun :*These women like me. - '''''Эти женщины'' любят меня.''' - Nom. of an animate, plural, feminine noun :*I like these women. - '''Я люблю ''этих женщин.''''' - Acc. of the noun So, masculine nouns denoting inanimate objects in the accusative case are the same as in the nominative case. If they're animated nouns, they follow the genitive rules, which are: add '''-а''', and replace '''-й''' and '''-ь''' with '''-я'''. Neuter nouns, regardless of animation, also keep their nominative forms in the accusative case. Feminine words are the only words to have their own accusative ending: '''-а''' becomes '''-у''', and '''-я''' becomes '''-ю'''. Feminine nouns ending in the soft sign '''-ь''' do not change. To form the plural of an inanimate word, use the nominative rules: add or replace with '''-ы''' or '''-и''', and neuter nouns change '''-o''' to '''-а''' and '''-e''' to '''-я'''. If the word is animate, regardless of gender, use the [[Russian/Grammar/Genitive case#Nouns|genitive plural]]: drop '''-а''' and '''-о''', convert or append ending consonants with '''-ов''', '''-ев''', or '''-ей''', and replace '''-я''' with '''-ь''' or '''-й'''. This summary table splits the masculine and plural forms into two sections, the left being the inanimate form, the right being the animate form. {| class="wikitable" |- ! ! colspan="2"|Masculine ! Feminine !! Neuter ! colspan="2"|Plural |- | Accusative || valign="bottom"|''As nom.'' || '''+a''', '''-я'''
''As gen.'' || valign="top"|'''у''', '''ю''', '''ь''' || '''о, е'''
''As nom.'' || '''ы, и, etc'''
''As nom.'' || '''ов, ев''', etc
''As gen.'' |} Examples: :* Dogs hate cats. - '''Собаки ненавидят котов.''' :* Cats hate dogs. - '''Коты ненавидят собак.''' :* I drove to the museum. - '''Я поехал в музей.'''

The supplied lines я читал — I was reading and я прочитал — I read are both past-tense forms with masculine singular agreement. The line я читал is imperfective past; the line я прочитал is perfective past. The first presents reading as activity or process; the second presents it as a completed whole. These English labels describe the retained examples; they are not a rule matching every English past tense to one Russian aspect.

Do not treat English past progressive and simple past as a fixed Russian aspect code. The imperfective does not always mean the action was unfinished. An activity may have ended and still be described imperfectively when the focus is its process or occurrence rather than its endpoint. Recognize the requested aspect in these supplied choices; this is not unrestricted sentence production.

чита́ть is the supplied infinitive; чита́л is its masculine singular past form. The dictionary label read names the recorded meaning and does not itself distinguish English past from infinitive. Compare the entire supplied forms. A question requesting masculine past asks for чита́л rather than feminine чита́ла; both past forms belong to the same imperfective verb.

чита́ла is the supplied feminine singular past form of чита́ть. Compare it with masculine чита́л. This contrast changes gender agreement, not aspect. Learn the supplied forms rather than inferring an unfamiliar ending or stress pattern.

На э́той у́лице есть францу́зы — There are Frenchmen on this street. This positive line states that something exists at the named place. It is a statement, not a question asking where something is. Recognize what exists and where the line places it.

В Москве́ есть ста́рые зда́ния — There are old buildings in Moscow. This line states that old buildings exist in Moscow. Compare its full meaning with the street example: the things and the named place differ. Keep each whole source line with its own supplied translation.

In both supplied positive statements, the noun naming what exists is nominative. Distinguish that noun from the location phrase. The previously introduced prepositional case is not the case of the noun naming what exists here. These two supplied examples do not establish an unrestricted sentence-generation rule.

provenanceRecords.shippedText:
The grammar page says: So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. An ending is not a substitute for the dictionary entry.

The dictionary lists these words as masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. учи́тель — teacher. The dictionary entry for друг — friend is also masculine. Learn the group with each word; an ending is not a substitute for the dictionary entry.

The dictionary lists these words as feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. ма́ма — mom. The dictionary entry for дверь — door is feminine. Learn the group with each word; do not guess the group of another word from its ending.

The dictionary lists these words as neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea. 

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

The dictionary lists these words as masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. учи́тель — teacher. The dictionary entry for друг — friend is also masculine. Learn the group with each word; an ending is not a substitute for the dictionary entry.

The dictionary lists these words as feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. ма́ма — mom. The dictionary entry for дверь — door is feminine. Learn the group with each word; do not guess the group of another word from its ending.

The dictionary lists these words as neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea. 

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

provenanceRecords.shippedText:
So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. Learn each word with its group; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. учи́тель — teacher. друг — friend is also masculine. Learn the group with each word; an ending alone does not decide it.

These words are feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. ма́ма — mom. дверь — door is feminine too. Learn the group with each word; do not guess the group of another word from its ending.

These words are neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea. 

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

In мой стол, the noun стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, the noun собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

Наш means our; Ваш means your (formal or plural). на́ша is the feminine singular nominative form of наш, and сестра́ is a feminine singular noun. In the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша becomes на́шу, and сестра́ becomes сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего is the masculine and neuter genitive form, and на́ши is plural.

тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. These choices test the requested form of the adjective; all the options are already correctly spelled.

After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, or щ, write и rather than ы. The seven-letter condition is required. This rule applies to the spelling of noun and adjective endings. In кни́ги, и follows г; in хоро́шие, и follows ш. Read the requested form before answering.

кни́га means book in the singular, and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. The stem ends in г, so the seven-letter rule requires и. In the other direction, кни́ги becomes кни́га in the singular nominative.

кни́ги is plural nominative in this lesson. дни is also plural nominative and means days. Its и does not follow a letter in the seven-letter set, so дни is not an example of that spelling replacement. Not every plural ending in и comes from the seven-letter rule. provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: numbers:The numeral один (1) should be used in the proper form to indicate gender (and,
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: The numeral один (1) should be used in the proper form to indicate gender (and, number, believe it or not).  For example: один мальчик (one boy), одна девушка (one girl), одно животное (one animal), одни джинсы (one [pair of] jeans).  The plural form of the numeral (1) is a bit of an oddity, but its use will become clear with time.  Following a form of один should come the item at hand in the nominative or inanimate accusative case, as appropriate.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: numbers:The numerals два (or две), три, and четыре all require the following item to be
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: The numerals два (or две), три, and четыре all require the following item to be presented in the genitive singular form.  The numeral два has two forms: два for masculine and neuter items and две for feminine items.  After the numeral два, each numeral has only a single form.  See for example:  две девушки (two girls), три кошки (three cats), четыре мальчика (four boys).

These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. A count ending in one outside the teen exception uses a nominative singular noun in the shown basic phrases. один час — один час. два часа — два часа.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: accusative:The accusative case is a peculiar case in Russian, as it makes a distinction tha
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: The accusative case is a peculiar case in Russian, as it makes a distinction that other cases do not. Specifically, if a masculine word denotes an inanimate thing ('table', 'chair', etc), then it remains the same as the nominative. If, however, a masculine word denotes a person or animal ('man', 'son', 'cow', etc), then the case uses the endings of the [[Russian/Grammar/Genitive case|''genitive case'']]. For plurals in the accusative, no matter what gender the word, they are also split: any plural word that's inanimate is identical to its [[Russian/Grammar/Nominative case|nominative plural form]], while animate plural words follow the rules for the genitive plural. Для него́ — For him/it. Без неё — Without her. 

For him/it - Для него́

Меня́ — I. Его́/её — He/she/it. 

Их — They. Я — I. 

Мы — We. Нас — We. 

Ты — You. Вы — You. 

Тебя́ — You. Вас — You.

In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? 

A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend. 

The many-friends example includes a quantity expression. Quantity patterns are separate from the simple nominative possessed thing. The no-son example below denies possession and uses the genitive for the absent thing. У моего нового мужа есть много друзе́й — My new husband has many friends. У меня́ нет сы́на — No, I don't have a son. 

The no-money example also denies possession. Choose the genitive absence explanation, rather than the simple positive possession explanation. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

новый карандаш is masculine singular nominative; новая машина is feminine singular nominative. The adjective agrees with the noun in the phrase, so the car phrase uses the feminine form но́вая rather than masculine но́вый or plural но́вые. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective но́вая becomes но́вую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Both words change in these supplied case pairs. In Анна встретила новую учительницу (Anna met the new teacher), the adjective новую and the noun учительницу are both accusative.

The dictionary form of this adjective is masculine singular nominative но́вый. A phrase can need another gender, number or case even though the dictionary form is masculine singular nominative. In the neuter, the adjective но́вое becomes но́вого in the genitive, and the noun окно́ becomes окна́. Both adjective and noun change case while remaining neuter singular. In Я пришёл из моего старого дома (I arrived from my old house), the words моего старого дома are all genitive.

новое платье is neuter singular nominative. Compare the adjective with the masculine pencil and feminine car examples above: the noun controls the agreement required in that phrase. синий стол uses the masculine nominative form of a different adjective meaning dark blue. один мальчик — one boy; одна девушка — one girl. For these singular counting examples, one agrees with the noun: masculine один and feminine одна. Both still mean one. Guided practice uses мальчик.

два is the form for masculine and neuter counted nouns; две is the feminine form. The supplied example две девушки — two girls uses feminine две. The following noun is genitive singular in this counting construction; the numeral choice still follows its gender.

одно животное — one animal uses neuter singular одно. одни джинсы — one [pair of] jeans uses plural одни with the plural-form noun. The plural numeral here does not mean several pairs; these are different gender/number forms of one.

одна́ and одно́ both represent 1 in the cardinal table. They are feminine and neuter singular forms, respectively.

одни́ represents 1 in the supplied plural-form example, while две represents 2 with a feminine noun. Distinguish одни джинсы from две девушки by the complete supplied construction, rather than treating every plural-looking form as two.

оди́н — one and два — two. The additional example один час uses masculine singular один with час; feminine singular одна is the form shown with девушка.

These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. A count ending in one outside the teen exception uses a nominative singular noun in the shown basic phrases. один час — один час. два часа — два часа. 

A count ending in two, three or four outside the teen exception uses a genitive singular noun in the basic construction. This is a grammatical singular form even though the count is greater than one.

Counts ending in zero or five through nine use genitive plural in the basic construction. The teen exception also uses genitive plural. Ten and sixteen therefore fit this pattern. пять часов — пять часов. двадцать один час — двадцать один час. 

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare 21 and 22: their final digits select different noun cases; being larger than five is not enough to choose genitive plural. двадцать два часа — двадцать два часа. две девушки — two girls. 

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. All counts from 11 through19 use genitive plural here. For 15 through19 the final digit already leads to genitive plural;11 through14 override the one/two/three/four ending pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles. 

The example with 41 follows the final-one pattern and uses nominative singular for the counted noun. The example with 10 follows the zero-ending pattern and uses genitive plural. десять копеек — ten kopeks. сорок один год — forty-one years. 

The count 203 ends in 03, so final three selects genitive singular in the basic counting phrase. The count 213 ends in 13, so the teen exception selects genitive plural. пять лет — пять лет. двести три собаки — two hundred and three dogs. 

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare the supplied 203 and 213 examples and the two kopeck examples. Read the whole example before answering. двести тринадцать собак — two hundred and thirteen dogs. Два́дцать две копе́йки — 22 kopecks. 

The isolated forms below illustrate genitive singular and genitive plural noun forms. Read the complete counting example. Два́дцать пять копе́ек — 25 kopecks. стола́ — table.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: grammar:The [[imperative mood]] second-person singular is formed from the future-present
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: The [[imperative mood]] second-person singular is formed from the future-present base of most verbs by adding -и (stressed ending in present-future, or if the base ends on more than one consonant), -ь (unstressed ending, base of one consonant) or -й (unstressed ending, base of vowel). The plural (including the polite ''на вы'') second-person form is made by adding -те to the singular one: говорю 'I speak' – говори – говорите, забуду 'I shall forget' – забудь – забудьте, клею 'I glue' – клей – клейте. Some perfective verbs have a first-person plural imperative form with -те added to a similar simple future or present tense form: пойдёмте 'let us go'. Other forms can express commands in Russian; for third person, for example, the particle пусть with future can be used: Пусть они замолчат! 'Let them shut up!'.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.russian-language-for-lovers.com/russian-verbs.html#five|title=Russian verbs: How to form the imperative}}</ref>

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: adjectives:#With plural nouns, regardless of gender, the adjective replaces '''-ый''' or ''
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: #With plural nouns, regardless of gender, the adjective replaces '''-ый''' or '''-ой''' with '''-ые''' ('ee-ye'), or it replaces '''-ий''' with '''-ие''' ('ee-ye'). For example, "these good new students" is '''эти хорошие новые студенты''' (pronounced ''<small>EH</small>-tee kha-<small>RO</small>-shee-ye <small>NO</small>-vih-yeh stoo-<small>DYENT</small>-ee''). As a memory aid, think of plural as one masculine and one neuter object. Take the first letter from the masculine ending ('''ы''') and the second letter from the neuter ending ('''e''') and you get '''ые'''.
provenanceRecords.shippedText: эти хорошие новые студенты

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: nominative:There is a spelling rule called the '7-letter spelling rule', so called because
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: There is a spelling rule called the '7-letter spelling rule', so called because it comes into effect after seven letters: '''к, г, х, ш, щ, ж''', and '''ч'''. When you remove the default ending from a word, you are left with the stem. If the stem ends in one of those seven letters, then you generally have to add an alternate ending. For example, '''книга''', 'book', has the stem '''книг-''', so it obeys the 7-letter rule. What to do when this spelling rule appears will be covered in each instance individually. However, the rule generally just requires the use of an 'alternate' noun ending.

provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: As mentioned earlier, if the stem of a noun ends in '''к''', '''г''', '''х''', '''ш''', '''щ''', '''ж''', and '''ч''', then different endings from usual apply. The same is true for adjectives. Adjectives such as '''хороший''' ('good'), '''русский''' ('Russian'), and '''другой''' ('different'), take on alternate endings to other adjectives. In an absence line, the absent thing is genitive. An absence line may describe what a person does not have or what does not exist at a place. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son. Нет рестора́нов — There are no restaurants. 

The absence construction uses a genitive noun for the absent thing. The simple positive possession construction instead uses a genitive possessor and a nominative possessed thing. Choose from the meaning and construction of the whole supplied line.

Both negative examples below use the genitive for the absent thing. Keep the absent thing separate from any possessor or place mentioned in the line. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money. 

The positive son example below affirms possession. Its possessed noun is nominative, so the genitive absence explanation does not classify this line. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son.

The absence construction uses a genitive noun for the absent thing. The simple positive possession construction instead uses a genitive possessor and a nominative possessed thing. Choose from the meaning and construction of the whole supplied line.

Both negative examples below use the genitive for the absent thing. Keep the absent thing separate from any possessor or place mentioned in the line. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? 

A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend. 

The many-friends example includes a quantity expression. Quantity patterns are separate from the simple nominative possessed thing. The no-son example below denies possession and uses the genitive for the absent thing. У моего нового мужа есть много друзе́й — My new husband has many friends. У меня́ нет сы́на — I don't have a son. 

The no-money example also denies possession. Choose the genitive absence explanation, rather than the simple positive possession explanation. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

In мой стол, the noun стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, the noun собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form.

Наш means our; Ваш means your (formal or plural). на́ша is the feminine singular nominative form of наш, and сестра́ is a feminine singular noun. In the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша becomes на́шу, and сестра́ becomes сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего is the masculine and neuter genitive form, and на́ши is plural.

тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

новый карандаш is masculine singular nominative; новая машина is feminine singular nominative. The adjective agrees with the noun in the phrase, so the car phrase uses the feminine form но́вая rather than masculine но́вый or plural но́вые. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective но́вая becomes но́вую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Both words change in these supplied case pairs. In Анна встретила новую учительницу (Anna met the new teacher), the adjective новую and the noun учительницу are both accusative.

The dictionary form of this adjective is masculine singular nominative но́вый. A phrase can need another gender, number or case even though the dictionary form is masculine singular nominative. In the neuter, the adjective но́вое becomes но́вого in the genitive, and the noun окно́ becomes окна́. Both adjective and noun change case while remaining neuter singular. In Я пришёл из моего старого дома (I arrived from my old house), the words моего старого дома are all genitive.

новое платье is neuter singular nominative. Compare the adjective with the masculine pencil and feminine car examples above: the noun controls the agreement required in that phrase. синий стол uses the masculine nominative form of a different adjective meaning dark blue. The comparison changes number; it does not change the adjective to a different vocabulary item.

An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective хоро́шая becomes хоро́шую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Keep the same noun when you change the case. хоро́шего is masculine singular genitive; хоро́шие is plural nominative. In Оно́ под хоро́шими кни́гами (It's under the good books), the adjective хоро́шими and the noun кни́гами are both instrumental plural.

хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший.

одно животное — one animal uses neuter singular одно. одни джинсы — one [pair of] jeans uses plural одни with the plural-form noun. The plural numeral here does not mean several pairs; these are different gender/number forms of one.

одна́ and одно́ both represent 1 in the cardinal table. They are feminine and neuter singular forms, respectively.

одни́ represents 1 in the supplied plural-form example, while две represents 2 with a feminine noun. Distinguish одни джинсы from две девушки by the complete supplied construction, rather than treating every plural-looking form as two.

оди́н — one and два — two. The additional example один час uses masculine singular один with час; feminine singular одна is the form shown with девушка.

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare 21 and 22: their final digits select different noun cases; being larger than five is not enough to choose genitive plural. двадцать два часа — twenty-two hours. две девушки — two girls.

provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: There are two important nuances to these pronouns. First, notice that the masculine and neuter third-person singular pronouns are the same in all cases but the nominative, and in the genitive and accusative are pronounced <nowiki>'</nowiki>''ye-vo''<nowiki>'</nowiki>, not <nowiki>'</nowiki>''ye-go''<nowiki>'</nowiki>. Second, if the pronoun's case is called by a preposition, third-person pronouns gain the prefix '''н-''' (e.g., compare 'his' in 'It's his house', '''Это его дом''', and 'He has a house', '''У него есть дом''').

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: past:Some verbs, such as the imperfective '''улыба́ться''' ('to smile'), have the ref
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: Some verbs, such as the imperfective '''улыба́ться''' ('to smile'), have the reflexive ending '''-сь/ся''' to indicate that the object is also the subject. Instead of saying 'I dress myself', Russians say 'I dress' and place the reflexive ending on the verb. Though not always reflexive in meaning (there is no verb '''улыбать''', and 'to smile' isn't reflexive in English, but Russians still use it reflexively), the ending nonetheless must be accounted for when forming the past tense. Similar to how reflexive verbs are conjugated in the present tense, you add the appropriate reflexive ending ''after'' forming the past tense.

To form the past tense, remove -ть from the infinitive and add -л. Add -ла if the subject is feminine, -ло if it is neuter and -ли if it is plural.

The past tense agrees with its subject in gender and number, not in person. Он чита́л — He was reading. Она чита́ла — She was reading. Они чита́ли — They were reading.

The past forms of быть, to be, follow the regular pattern: бы́л for a masculine subject, была́ for a feminine subject, бы́ло for a neuter subject and бы́ли for a plural subject. Он был в Москве́ — He was in Moscow. Она была́ краси́вая — She was beautiful.

Some verbs, such as идти, have irregular past forms that cannot be predicted.

A reflexive verb such as улыба́ться, to smile, has a reflexive ending. To form its past tense, remove the reflexive ending, form the past tense, then reattach the ending: -ся after a consonant and -сь after a vowel.

Он улыба́лся — He was smiling. Она улыба́лась — She was smiling. Они улыба́лись — They were smiling.

The verb meaning to study follows the same pattern: учи́лся for a masculine subject, учи́лась for a feminine subject and учи́лись for a plural subject.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: grammatical-aspect:In European languages, rather than locating an event time, the way tense does, a
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: In European languages, rather than locating an event time, the way tense does, aspect describes "the internal temporal constituency of a situation", or in other words, aspect is a way "of conceiving the flow of the process itself".<ref name=Comrie>Bernard Comrie, 1976. ''Aspect''. Cambridge University Press</ref> English aspectual distinctions in the past tense include "I went, I used to go, I was going, I had gone"; in the present tense "I lose, I am losing, I have lost, I have been losing, I am going to lose"; and with the future modal "I will see, I will be seeing, I will have seen, I am going to see". What distinguishes these aspects within each tense is not (necessarily) when the event occurs, but how the time in which it occurs is viewed: as complete, ongoing, consequential, planned, etc.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: grammatical-aspect:In [[linguistics]], '''aspect''' is a [[grammatical category]] that expresses ho
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: In [[linguistics]], '''aspect''' is a [[grammatical category]] that expresses how a [[verb|verbal]] action, event, or state, extends over time. For instance, [[perfective aspect]] is used in referring to an event conceived as [[boundedness (linguistics)|bounded]] and only once occurring, without reference to any flow of time during the event ("I helped him"). [[Imperfective aspect]] is used for situations conceived as existing continuously or habitually as time flows ("I was helping him"; "I used to help people").

provenanceRecords.shippedText: Essentially, the perfective aspect looks at an event as a complete action, while the imperfective aspect views an event as the process of unfolding or a repeated or habitual event (thus corresponding to the progressive/continuous aspect for events of short-term duration and to habitual aspect for longer terms).

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: aspect:All verbs in Russian have an aspect. Some verbs exist in aspectual pairs, but ce
provenanceRecords.shippedText: All verbs in Russian have an aspect. Some verbs exist in aspectual pairs, but certainly not most of them. In the case of an aspectual pair, one word is the imperfective aspect of that verb, and the other is the perfective aspect. Very roughly, the imperfective aspect is used when the action is incomplete, or when the focus is in the process of the action, while the perfective aspect is used either when the action ''is'' complete or the focus is in the completion of the action or its outcome.

provenanceRecords.shippedText: However, one has to be careful with prefixes. For instance, we can add the prefix '''от''' to the imperfective '''говорить''' to make the new perfective '''отговорить''', meaning 'to dissuade'. provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: prepositional:The two plural endings, '''ах''' and '''ях''', follow the same rules as the [[Ru
provenanceRecords.shippedText: The two plural endings, '''ах''' and '''ях''', follow the same rules as the [[Russian/Grammar/Instrumental case|instrumental]] and [[Russian/Grammar/Dative case|dative]] plurals: after consonants, '''o''', or '''а''', use the ending '''ах'''. If such a noun has an irregular nominative plural ending in '''я''' (e.g., '''друг''' --> '''друзья'''), or if the noun ends in '''ь''', '''й''', '''е''', or '''я''', the ending is '''ях''' (e.g., '''друг''' --> '''друзья''' --> '''друзьях''').

provenanceRecords.shippedText: Imperfective verbs form the future by preceding the imperfective infinitive with the appropriate conjugation of the perfective verb '''быть'''. provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: verbs:Like English verbs, Russian verbs also conjugate according to who is doing the v
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: Like English verbs, Russian verbs also conjugate according to who is doing the verb: when on its own the default ''infinitive'' form corresponds to the English 'to' ('to see', 'to walk', etc), and this infinitive can conjugate for each of the six [[Russian/Personal Pronouns|personal pronouns]] - '''я''' ('I'), '''мы''' ('we'), '''ты''' ('you', informal), '''вы''' ('you', plural/polite), '''он/она/оно''' ('he/she/it'), and '''они''' ('they'). Notice that although the third-person singular pronoun has three forms for each gender, there is still only one third-person singular form of a verb, just as in English. The other thing to note is that Russian has two words for 'you' like French and German, but unlike modern English. Briefly, '''ты''' is used informally for a single person who you know well, while '''вы''' is used for groups of people, or for an individual person to whom you want to show respect.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: adjectives:Adjectives in Russian are simply words that modify nouns. The endings of adjecti
provenanceRecords.shippedText: Adjectives in Russian are simply words that modify nouns. The endings of adjectives change according to the gender, number, and case of the nouns they modify. The rules for changing adjectives is often a lot easier than the rules for changing nouns themselves. There are six cases, and so six main ways of conjugating adjectives to fit the noun they modify. Finally, there are the ''short adjectives'', detailed at the end.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: prepositional:Words decline into a case for two broad reasons: because they match that case's
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: Words decline into a case for two broad reasons: because they match that case's primary function (the [[Russian/Grammar/Nominative|nominative]] denotes the verbal subject, the [[Russian/Grammar/Accusative case|accusative]] denotes the verbal object, etc), or because they come after a preposition that governs that particular case ('''у''' governs the [[Russian/Grammar/Genitive case|genitive]], '''между''' governs the [[Russian/Grammar/Instrumental case|instrumental]], etc). The prepositional case is so called because it is only ever used after prepositions. Historically, the prepositional case was called the ''locative'' case as its primary function was to denote the location of something. This use has been taken over by prepositions, so its name was changed accordingly. However, you may still hear it referred to by its old name, and some words still bear hallmarks of the old locative case.

Aspect describes how an action is viewed, not when it happens. Imperfective can present an action as a process or as a repeated or habitual event. Perfective presents an event with its boundary or result. Imperfective does not by itself mean unfinished. говори́ть is imperfective; сказа́ть is perfective. Learn the two supplied infinitives.

Many Russian verbs are learned in an aspect pair, but not every verb has two words, and a pair is not automatic. говорить and сказать are context-dependent counterparts, not a universal pair for the English verb speak. For the saying/telling pair shown here, the perfective counterpart of говори́ть is сказа́ть; the imperfective counterpart of сказа́ть is говори́ть.

де́лать is imperfective; сде́лать is perfective. Both concern doing or making. The perfective presents the action as a complete whole; the imperfective presents it as a process. говори́ть concerns speaking or saying and belongs to the other pair. Learn the shown pair rather than assuming every prefix changes only aspect.

To form the present tense, add the appropriate endings to the verb. Verbs in Russian conjugate in one of two ways.

чита́ть in the present: I чита́ю, you чита́ешь, he чита́ет. 

чита́ть in the present: we чита́ем, you (plural) чита́ете, they чита́ют. 

де́лать — make. With I: де́лаю.

More infinitives: знать — know. рабо́тать — work. понима́ть — understand. слу́шать — listen. 

More infinitives: жить — live. говори́ть — to speak. ви́деть — see. смотре́ть — look. 

More infinitives: писа́ть — write. идти́ — go. 

The infinitive говори́ть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: говорю́; you (one familiar person): говори́шь; he: говори́т; we: говори́м. Compare the written endings in these supplied forms; do not substitute the endings from the earlier reading example.

The infinitive ви́деть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: ви́жу; you (one familiar person): ви́дишь; he: ви́дит; we: ви́дим. The infinitive alone does not tell you which supplied form to choose. Notice that the I form differs from the other forms here; learn the whole supplied forms.

The infinitive писа́ть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: пишу́; you (one familiar person): пи́шешь; he: пи́шет; you (plural): пи́шете. The supplied present forms have a different written stem from the infinitive. Keep the written stress exactly as shown; do not append an ending to the whole infinitive.

The infinitive идти́ names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: иду́; you (one familiar person): идёшь; he: идёт; they: иду́т. The supplied finite forms differ from the infinitive. Learn these whole forms; this lesson does not teach how to choose between motion verbs in context.

To form the present tense, add the appropriate endings to the verb. Verbs in Russian conjugate in one of two ways.

чита́ть in the present: I чита́ю, you чита́ешь, he чита́ет. 

чита́ть in the present: we чита́ем, you (plural) чита́ете, they чита́ют. 

де́лать — make. With I: де́лаю.

More infinitives: знать — know. рабо́тать — work. понима́ть — understand. слу́шать — listen. 

More infinitives: жить — live. говори́ть — to speak. ви́деть — see. смотре́ть — look. 

More infinitives: писа́ть — write. идти́ — go. 

The infinitive говори́ть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: говорю́; you (one familiar person): говори́шь; he: говори́т; we: говори́м. Compare the written endings in these supplied forms; do not substitute the endings from the earlier reading example.

The infinitive ви́деть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: ви́жу; you (one familiar person): ви́дишь; he: ви́дит; we: ви́дим. The infinitive alone does not tell you which supplied form to choose. Notice that the I form differs from the other forms here; learn the whole supplied forms.

The infinitive писа́ть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: пишу́; you (one familiar person): пи́шешь; he: пи́шет; you (plural): пи́шете. The supplied present forms have a different written stem from the infinitive. Keep the written stress exactly as shown; do not append an ending to the whole infinitive.

The infinitive идти́ names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: иду́; you (one familiar person): идёшь; he: идёт; they: иду́т. The supplied finite forms differ from the infinitive. Learn these whole forms; practise choosing motion verbs in context separately.

In the supplied Муж говорит, the husband is the subject and the talking verb states its action. The noun names the subject, in the nominative case. Distinguish the noun’s subject or direct-object role from the meaning of the sentence. Do not guess nominative merely because a case is unfamiliar.

In Поезд старый, the train is the subject noun and old is its predicate description. This present property clause has no overt Russian copula. The noun’s case role is nominative subject, not accusative direct object. A dictionary-looking noun or familiar translation alone does not identify its role in every construction.

Студент новый supplies a second independent property clause: the student is the subject noun, and new describes that subject. Its case role is nominative subject. Keep Муж говорит — The husband is talking and Поезд старый — The train is old as correct sentence meanings. Other constructions have nominative predicate nouns; not every nominative noun is a subject.

кни́га means book in the singular, and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. New text: "один мальчик — one boy; одна девушка — one girl. For these singular counting examples, one agrees with the noun: masculine один and feminine одна. Both still mean one.

одно животное — one animal uses neuter singular одно. одни джинсы — one [pair of] jeans uses plural одни with the plural-form noun. The plural numeral here does not mean several pairs; these are different gender/number forms of one.

одна́ and одно́ both represent 1. They are feminine and neuter singular forms, respectively.

одни́ represents 1 in the supplied plural-form example, while две represents 2 with a feminine noun. Distinguish одни джинсы from две девушки by the complete supplied construction, rather than treating every plural-looking form as two.

оди́н — one and два — two. The additional example один час uses masculine singular один with час; feminine singular одна is the form shown with девушка."

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: past:Forming the Russian past tense is relatively straightforward, but first we have
provenanceRecords.shippedText: Forming the Russian past tense is relatively straightforward, but first we have to decide which aspect of the verb we want to use. As discussed in [[Russian/Verbal_Aspect|Verbal Aspect]], the imperfective aspect of verbs is used for incomplete or indefinitely repeated actions, while perfective aspects are for completed actions, or actions repeated a known number of times. These correspond roughly with the past progressive ('I was verbing') and the simple past ('I verbed'), respectively. So the English ''past progressive'' sentence  "I was reading" would correspond to the Russian imperfective ('''я читал'''), since it refers to an action that wasn't completed. Likewise, the English ''simple past'' sentence "I read" corresponds to the Russian perfective ('''я прочитал'''), as it refers to an action that ''was'' completed:

provenanceRecords.shippedText: All verbs in Russian have an aspect. Some verbs exist in aspectual pairs, but certainly not most of them. In the case of an aspectual pair, one word is the imperfective aspect of that verb, and the other is the perfective aspect. Very roughly, the imperfective aspect is used when the action is incomplete, or when the focus is in the process of the action, while the perfective aspect is used either when the action ''is'' complete or the focus is in the completion of the action or its outcome.

provenanceRecords.shippedText: Essentially, the perfective aspect looks at an event as a complete action, while the imperfective aspect views an event as the process of unfolding or a repeated or habitual event (thus corresponding to the progressive/continuous aspect for events of short-term duration and to habitual aspect for longer terms).

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: future:There is also the decision whether to use the future tense at all, and there are
provenanceRecords.shippedText: There is also the decision whether to use the future tense at all, and there are three nuances between English and Russian. In English, when reporting a story, we usually change the tense of what was said: compare "I ''am'' English" with "He said he ''was'' English" - the reported verb changes tense. In Russian, however, we keep the tense the same, so the same report is literally, "He said he '''is''' English" - "'''Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин'''", not "'''Он сказа́л, что он ''был'' англича́нином'''". Whatever tense was used originally is kept.

provenanceRecords.shippedText: However, one has to be careful with prefixes. While the perfective can be formed by a prefix, other prefixes can be applied to an imperfective to make a whole new verbal pair. For instance, we can add the prefix '''от''' to the imperfective '''говорить''' to make the new perfective '''отговорить''', meaning 'to dissuade'. From this, we can derive a new imperfective aspect, '''отговаривать'''. provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: sequence-of-tenses:A hypothetical context in which rules of sequence of tenses apply is that of [[i
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: A hypothetical context in which rules of sequence of tenses apply is that of [[indirect speech]]. If, at some past time, someone spoke a sentence in a particular tense (say the present tense), and that act of speaking is now being reported, the tense used in the clause that corresponds to the words spoken may or may not be the same as the tense that was used by the original speaker. In some languages the tense tends to be "shifted back", so that what was originally spoken in the present tense is reported using the past tense (since what was in the present at the time of the original sentence is in the past relative to the time of reporting). [[English grammar|English]] is one of the languages in which this often occurs. For example, if someone said "I '''need''' a drink", this may be reported in the form "She said she '''needed''' a drink", with the tense of the verb ''need'' changed from present to past.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: future:Another nuance between English and Russian is using prepositions and time. In En
provenanceRecords.shippedText: Another nuance between English and Russian is using prepositions and time. In English, after 'if', 'until', 'while', 'when', etc, we use the present tense, even if we're referring to the future. For example, in "If I fly, I'll phone you", "I fly" is the present tense, even though we're referring to the future. Since Russian has less ambiguous grammar for tense and aspect, if they're referring to the future with those words, they use it: "If I ''will fly'', I'll phone you" - '''Если я ''полечу́'', Я тебе́ позвоню́'''.

The line я читал is imperfective past; the line я прочитал is perfective past. The first presents reading as activity or process; the second presents it as a completed whole. These English labels describe the examples; they do not match every English past tense to one Russian aspect.

Do not treat English past progressive and simple past as a fixed Russian aspect code. The imperfective does not always mean the action was unfinished. Learn the supplied forms rather than inferring an unfamiliar ending or stress pattern.

Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин has a past said verb and no past copula in the nationality statement. The supplied original is “I am English”. It has a past reporting verb with a present nationality statement. The alternative with a past copula changes the stated reading. Review the nationality example you learned earlier.

Я скажу ему ве́чером is the direct statement “I will tell him in the evening”. Она́ сказа́ла, что она́ ска́жет ему́ ве́чером is the supplied reported evening context. It has a past reporting verb with a future embedded action. The reporting verb said is past, and the embedded telling action keeps its future form. Russian indirect speech generally keeps the tense of the original statement. Use the supplied examples.

Когда́ я бу́ду в Москве́, я бу́ду говори́ть то́лько по-ру́сски gives a future time clause and a plan to speak Russian. It has no past reporting frame. Distinguish the Moscow plan from the direct evening statement. In the evening report, distinguish the past reporting verb from the future embedded action. English backshift is not compulsory in every report; preserving these readings is not a universal rule that every tense or word stays unchanged. Study these examples in context; practise creating reports separately.

Keeping the tense the same describes this Russian reporting comparison; it does not mean every verb in a report has the same tense. The direct evening statement is Я скажу ему ве́чером. In this comparison, English can shift a present statement to a past form after a past reporting verb. The label we usually change the tense names that English backshift comparison. provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: ruwiki-vid:Категория вида близка категории [[способ действия|способа действия]] (''Aktionsa
provenanceRecords.originalSourceText: Категория вида близка категории [[способ действия|способа действия]] (''Aktionsart'', акциональности), связанной с тем, какая информация о способе протекания действия содержится в [[лексическое значение|лексическом значении]] [[глагол]]а (например, русские глаголы ''закричать'', ''залаять'' имеют значение начинательного способа глагольного действия, глаголы ''поспать'', ''почитать'' — ограничительного способа действия). Кроме того, могут быть значения результативности ([[результатив]]), делания чего-либо до конца, до завершения ([[комплетив]]), однократности, многократности ([[фреквентатив]]), привычности, традиционности состояния ([[хабитуалис]]), прерывистости, сопроводительности и др.)

provenanceRecords.shippedText: Forming the future tense with perfective verbs is relative straight-forward: just conjugate the verb according to the standard rules of verbal conjugation. The compound future puts a future form of быть before the imperfective infinitive, and the form of быть agrees with the subject. быть itself is an imperfective verb.

Different letters, same final sound

At the end of a word said on its own, a voiced consonant letter is pronounced like its voiceless partner: г like к, д like т. So луг (meadow) and лук (onion) end in the same sound, as do код (code) and кот (cat), and плод (fruit) and плот (raft). The spelling keeps the letter, so read the letter to know the word. sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
Грамматика: At what time on the quarter hour

Time Explanation and examples
At what time on the hour (0.00) Use в + accusative, but note that the number then often requires genitive case after it. In informal speech, sometimes people leave out час / часа / часов. Remember: один час; два / три / четыре часа; пять часов.

Концерт начинается в шесть часов. (18.00)
Она была дома в час. (13.00)
At what time on the quarter hour (0.15) Use в + accusative with either четверть (quarter) or пятнадцать минут. Then you use the ordinal number of the next hour in the genitive case. In essence you are saying quarter of the next hour. Note that while you can say 6:15 as “шесть пятнадцать”, in the exercises on this page we would like to focus on this other way of expressing the time.

Я приду в четверть восьмого. (7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour)
Он нам позвонил в пятнадцать минут десятого. (9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour)

If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:
At what time on the half hour (0.30) Use в + prepositional with половина and the genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour, or colloquially, пол_____ (genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour). Note that the spelling of 10:30 adds a hyphen: пол-одиннадцатого.

Наш рейс уезжает в половине пятого. (4.30 – half of the fifth hour)
Мы будем свободны в полвторого. (1.30 – half of the second hour)

If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:
At what time on the three quarters hour (0.45) Use без + genitive with четверть or пятнадцать минут. Then you use the cardinal number of the next hour in the nominative case. In essence you are saying X hours without X minutes.

Передача начинается без четверти три. (2.45 – 3 without a quarter)
Она обычно приходит на работу без пятнадцати девять. (8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes)

sourceCapabilities.sourceRecordId: grammar20:We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the
sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the number of whole hours and minutes which have passed since noon or midnight. This option is always available.
In Russian we can state the number of minutes into the hour which is in progress. This makes sense up to the half hour.
We can say how many minutes remain until the little hand passes the next number on the dial. This is used after the half hour.
We can speak of quarters and halves of an hour rather than of minutes.
If the precise time is not important, then in Russian we can say things like “at the beginning of the hour” to indicate a time close to the start of the our or “at the end of the hour” for a time near its end.

The concept of the hour in progress will be unfamiliar to most English speakers. It is important to understand that “the first hour” does not mean one o'clock. It means the sixty-minute period which starts at 12 o'clock and ends at one o'clock. In the examples below the hour in progress is represented by a shaded pie slice.

The first hour began at 12 o'clock. To say that something happens at the time shown at left:
в двенадцать часов десять минут—at twelve hours ten minutes
в десять минут первого—at ten minutes of the first
в начале первого часа—at the beginning of the first hour

As the little hand passes the 1 the first hour ends and the second begins. To specify this time use any of these expressions:
в час пятнадцать минут—at [one] hour fifteen minutes
в пятнадцать минут второго—at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

в час двадцать пять минут—at [one] hour twenty five minutes
в двадцать пять минут второго—at twenty five minutes of the second [hour]

Once the hour is half-way done we may choose to say how soon the little hand will pass the next number. To specify the time shown at left:
в час тридцать пять минут—at [one] hour thirty five minutes
без двадцати пяти два—lacking twenty five minutes to the two

sourceCapabilities.sourceRecordId: date-russia:In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This o
sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.17}}") and the expanded form (for example "{{lang|ru|28 августа 2017 г.}}"); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (''goda'', "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.2017}}") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral [[grammatical gender]]), then the month in [[genitive case]] (for example "{{lang|ru|Двадцать восьмое августа}}").

sourceCapabilities.sourceRecordId: grammar:forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and sup
sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.

Современная иллюстрированная энциклопедия|ответственный=Горкин А.П.|год=2006|язык=ru|место=Москва|издательство=Росмен|страницы=611}}</ref>. sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
Note that the modifier не negates the word which comes right after it. If you were to move it in front of a different word, you would produce a different meaning. For example:

Мне не холодно.

To me it is not cold. (I am not cold.)

Не мне холодно.

It is not to me that it is cold. (I am not the one who thinks it is cold.)

sourceCapabilities.sourceRecordId: lichnoe-imya:В словообразовании уменьшительных и ласкательных форм имён участвуют разнообразн
sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
В словообразовании уменьшительных и ласкательных форм имён участвуют разнообразные [[диминутив]]ные суффиксы (-очк-, -ечк-, -оньк-, -еньк-, -ушк-, -юшк-, -юш-, -яш-, -уш-, -ул-, -ун-, -ус-, -к-, -ик, и другие), а в качестве основ используются как основы полных имён, так и кратких форм. Например, от полной формы имени ''Мария'' и ''Марья'' образуются уменьшительные ''Марюня, Маруня, Маруся, Марюша'' и ''Марьюшка, Марьяша''; от краткой формы ''Маша → Машка, Машенька, Машуля''; от краткой формы ''Маня → Манечка, Манюся, Манюша, Маняша'' и т. п. Выбор [[диминутив]]ной формы имени зависит от полноты чувства, испытываемого говорящим по отношению к именуемому; учитывая разнообразие основ, обусловленное множеством кратких форм, и суффиксов, уменьшительные и ласкательные имена позволяют выразить в речи широкий спектр эмоциональных красок<ref name="ОРИ-5" />.

Уменьшительные имена, образованные при помощи суффикса -к-, несут в себе оттенок пренебрежения, умаления достоинства именуемого (''Сашка, Гришка, Светка'' и т. п.). Исторически это связано с существовавшей традицией использовать уже упоминавшиеся [[Полуимя|полуимена]] (которые как раз образовывались с помощью суффикса -к-) для самоуничижения при обращении к лицу из привилегированного сословия<ref group="с">Социальную сниженность, пренебрежительность подобных имён остро чувствовал [[Белинский, Виссарион Григорьевич|В. Г. Белинский]]:{{начало цитаты}}[Россия] представляет собою ужасное зрелище страны, где люди торгуют людьми, <…> страны, где люди сами себя называют не именами, а кличками: Ваньками, Стешками, Васьками, Палашками.{{конец цитаты|источник=[[s:Письмо Н. В. Гоголю (Белинский)|В. Г. Белинский. «Письмо Н. В. Гоголю»]]}}</ref>. Однако среди простого народа при общении равных по социальному положению людей эта форма имён, как правило, не имела такого оттенка, свидетельствуя лишь о простоте обращения и очевидной близости. Тем не менее в современном [[Русский язык|русском языке]] [[диминутив]]ные имена наподобие ''Васька, Маринка, Алка'' считаются стилистически приниженными

sourceCapabilities.sourceRecordId: obraschenie:Есть полные имена — Ирина, Евгения, Александр и др., сокращённые или краткие име
sourceCapabilities.exactSpan:
Есть полные имена — Ирина, Евгения, Александр и др., сокращённые или краткие имена — Ира, Женя, Саша и др., а также уменьшительно-ласкательные — Ирочка, Женечка, Сашенька и др.

Обращение по [[Полное имя|полному имени]] характерно для отстранённо-официального регистра общения, используется в официальной или полуофициальной обстановке общения, выражает подчёркнуто сдержанное отношение к собеседнику и чаще всего используется, когда предстоит серьёзный разговор, необходимо сделать замечание собеседнику: «Сергей, мне надо с тобой поговорить», «Татьяна, подойди сюда».

Краткие формы имён используются в дружески-неофициальном общении со знакомыми, родственниками одного возраста
